title: Name the category norm a wild bet breaks before you design it
hypothesis: If we can name the exact category norm a bet breaks and the adjacent industry it borrows from, then the bet is more likely to feel like a real point of view instead of a copy of another brand's stunt.
does_not_apply_when: It is a standard tactic (percent off, BOGO, free shipping, points, an abandoned-cart email) with no twist

signal.check: The team wants to run a wild bet but cannot state, in one sentence, the norm it breaks or the industry it borrows the idea from.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source measures this, it is a design filter

risk.note: A naming exercise on paper; nothing goes to a customer yet.

prerequisites: Brand voice statement on file
steps: List the unwritten rules of the category (never link off the site, discounts are the only urgency lever, points never expire).
Pick the one rule that feels most constraining to this brand right now.
Name one adjacent industry (luxury drops, hospitality, gaming, collectibles) whose model could break that rule here.
Write both in one sentence and attach it to the bet brief before any other design work starts.

test.method: Not a test on its own; a gate the bet brief must pass before P1 continues.
test.measure: Whether the brief names a norm and a model
test.read_point: Before the approval request is drafted

title: Run a faucet test before picking any wild bet
hypothesis: If we measure organic vs paid revenue share, or run a bounded no-ads week, then we learn whether this brand is paid-dependent before spending time on a bet that assumes an owned audience.
does_not_apply_when: A brand with strong paid economics may stay ad-led on purpose; the test sizes dependence, it does not condemn it

signal.check: No one can say what share of last year's revenue came from organic vs paid channels.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this is a diagnostic, not a lift

risk.note: A read of existing data; no live change to the store.

prerequisites: 12 months of weekly organic vs paid revenue by week
steps: Pull weekly organic and paid revenue for the last 12 months.
Compute the organic share of total revenue by week and the trend.
If the number cannot be trusted, plan a bounded no-ads week instead (see the no-ads week idea).
Use the result to size how much a wild bet program even matters for this brand yet.

test.method: Compare organic share over time; re-check quarterly.
test.read_point: Once, before the quarterly wild bets plan, then quarterly

title: Fund only one wild bet lever per quarter from a shared cash cap
hypothesis: If we fund one wild bet lever per quarter from one shared cash cap instead of splitting it across the discount ladder, loyalty and a drop at once, then each cohort stays clean for a control read.

signal.check: More than one unbounded program (a new loyalty mechanic, a discount test, a drop) is being planned for the same quarter with no shared cap.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this is a design rule, not a measured lift

risk.note: A planning decision; does not touch customers directly.

prerequisites: Quarterly cash cap and labor hours set by the owner
steps: List every program planned to touch the same or overlapping cohorts this quarter.
Pick one wild bet lever for this quarter's cash cap.
Check that no other play (loyalty change, drop, discount test) runs on the same cohort in the same window.
Record the choice and the runners-up not chosen, with the reason.

test.method: Review the quarterly plan for cohort overlap before approval.
test.measure: Number of programs touching the same cohort in the window

title: Cap the quarter's wild bet downside to a share of contribution margin
hypothesis: If we size the quarter's wild bets so that all of them failing stays under an agreed share of quarterly contribution margin, then a bad quarter for wild bets cannot threaten the business.

signal.check: The wild bet cash cap for the quarter was picked without checking it against contribution margin, not revenue.

expected_effect.size: worst case, all 3 bets fail: the source asks what is the worst case and whether it can be hedged, but gives no percentage

risk.note: A budgeting step; the risk is in the bets themselves, not this check.

prerequisites: Quarterly contribution margin figure
steps: Pull the quarter's forecast contribution margin.
Set the wild bet cash cap as a share of that margin the owner is comfortable losing entirely.
Write the worst-case scenario for each bet and confirm it fits inside the cap.
Cap any single bet at half the shared quarterly cap so one bet cannot use it all.

test.method: Recompute total exposure whenever a bet is added or resized.
test.measure: Total cash cap as a percent of quarterly contribution margin
test.read_point: At quarterly planning and before each new bet is added

title: Borrow a play model from an industry outside ecommerce, not from other DTC brands
hypothesis: If we deliberately borrow a mechanic from luxury drops, hospitality, gaming or collectibles instead of copying another DTC brand's tactic, then the play is harder for a direct competitor to copy quickly.

signal.check: Every wild bet idea on the table is a version of something a direct competitor already does.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the sources give named examples, not a lift

risk.note: An ideation input; the risk sits in whatever play is finally chosen.

prerequisites: Brand voice and margin checks passed (see the voice-fit and values-backed ideas)
steps: Pick one adjacent industry: luxury fashion drops, gaming FOMO, hospitality service, live events, collectibles, or financial-market hedges.
Ask what that industry's core mechanic is and whether it survives the brand's margin and voice.
Sketch a scaled-down version sized to this brand's cash and labor.
Take the sketch into the normal bet design process.

test.method: Not tested on its own; feeds into the bound bet's own control and readout.
test.measure: Whichever metric the resulting bet's bound names
test.read_point: At the resulting bet's review date

title: Check brand voice fit before running a stunt or absurd play
hypothesis: If the owner confirms in writing that a stunt or absurdist play matches the brand's actual voice, then the play reads as the brand instead of confusing customers with a format that does not fit.
does_not_apply_when: A serious, considered-purchase brand voice; run hospitality or status plays instead of punk stunts

signal.check: A stunt or absurd idea is on the table and no one has written down whether it matches the brand's voice.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources warn that copying the format without the voice usually flops, no figure given

risk.note: A written confirmation step, before anything is built or spent.

prerequisites: A written brand voice statement (irreverent or serious)
steps: Describe the planned stunt or absurd play in one paragraph.
Have the owner confirm in writing whether it matches the brand's actual voice, not the voice the team wishes it had.
If it does not fit, swap to a hospitality, status or values play instead.
Attach the confirmation to the bet brief.

test.method: Not a test; a gate before P18 continues.
test.read_point: Before the legal and brand-risk review

title: Document every wild bet's result, win or lose
hypothesis: If every wild bet ends in a written registry entry with what was done, why, and the numbers, then the next bet can repeat what worked instead of starting from a one-off story that fades.

signal.check: Past wild bets or gestures exist only as anecdotes the team remembers, with no written record of cohort, cost or result.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source measures this, it is a documentation practice

risk.note: Paperwork; no customer-facing risk.

prerequisites: A place to store registry entries (brand record or spreadsheet)
steps: At the end of every bet, write the registry entry fields: hypothesis, cohort, cash and labor spent, metric result, decision, and what changes next time.
File it even when the bet failed or was never launched.
Review filed entries before designing the next bet in the same lever.
Turn a policy that worked (not just a one-off gesture) into a standing rule.

test.method: Check the registry before every new bet design.
test.measure: Share of past bets with a filed registry entry

title: Only run a values or cultural play when a real program backs the message
hypothesis: If a values or cultural message is only run when the brand can point to a real program behind it (repair, resale, a documented policy), then the message reads as authentic instead of drawing greenwashing accusations.
does_not_apply_when: The values program does not exist yet, or the cultural moment would not read as authentic to this brand's customers

signal.check: A values or cultural message is planned but no program (repair, resale, a documented policy) exists behind it yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source's example (Patagonia's anti-consumption ad backed by repair and resale) is a case, not a rate

risk.note: A faked or unbacked values message can draw public backlash that is hard to walk back.

prerequisites: A documented program the message can point to
steps: Write the values or cultural message the team wants to run.
Ask: what program exists today that backs this message?
If no program exists, do not run the message; build the program first or drop the play.
If a program exists, cite it plainly in the message so it is not just a claim.

test.method: Legal, ethics and brand-risk review before the message goes public (see the stunt review idea).
test.measure: Complaints, backlash mentions, and sales in the window vs a matched period
test.read_point: Immediately after launch and again at the campaign window's close

title: Keep human, one-to-one moments manual and automate only the rule-based work around them
hypothesis: If the founder or team keeps notes, referral asks and over-delivery manual while letting automation handle triggers, logging and reminders, then the manual work keeps giving insight a dashboard cannot, while nothing important falls through the cracks.

signal.check: A tool or AI feature is about to replace a personal follow-up, referral ask or over-delivery moment instead of just the logging around it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source measures this directly, it is a stated tension the sources resolve the same way

risk.note: A staffing and workflow decision, not a customer-facing change on its own.

prerequisites: A list of current manual touches and any automation being considered for them
steps: List every manual touch currently run by hand (notes, calls, referral asks, gifts).
For each, decide whether automation would replace the human moment or just the logging around it.
Automate only the logging, reminders and triggers.
Graduate a play to a system only after it has passed two controlled reads (see the staged rollout idea).

test.method: Track whether reorder and referral rates hold after any automation change to a manual play.
test.measure: repeat_rate_90d, referral share, before vs after automating part of the play

title: Start any manual wild bet on the smallest group the team can serve by hand
hypothesis: If a manual delight play starts with the smallest group the team can serve well by hand, then each recipient gets real attention and the play feels personal instead of diluted.
does_not_apply_when: A mass program aimed at pleasing everyone a little

signal.check: A manual play is being scoped for a group larger than the team can realistically give personal attention to.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no case number given, this is a design principle

risk.note: Sizing decision only; widen later on a passed gate.

prerequisites: Customer list ranked by lifetime spend
Labor hours available for manual touches
steps: Rank customers by lifetime spend.
Pick the smallest group the team can serve by hand this month (often 10 to 50).
Run the play on that group only, with a control.
Widen to a larger cohort only after the smaller group beats its control.

test.method: Compare treated vs control repeat and reorder rate at the review date.
test.read_point: At the play's planned review date, typically 90 days

title: Prove a new experience or VIP segment works by hand before automating it
hypothesis: If we prove the value of a new experience or a new VIP segment with manual effort first, then we only spend on automation and ads once we know the underlying idea actually works.

signal.check: The team is about to build automated infrastructure (a tool, an app, a workflow) for an experience that has not yet been proven by hand with real customers.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources cite manual, hand-run proof cases as illustrations, not rates

risk.note: Manual work only; nothing is automated or built yet.

prerequisites: Founder or team time to run the experience manually for a small group
steps: Pick the smallest version of the new experience or VIP segment that can be run entirely by hand.
Run it personally for a handful of real customers.
Log what worked, what customers said, and any reorder or referral signal.
Only then decide whether to build a system or tool around it.

test.method: Track reorder and referral for the hand-run group informally before any formal control exists.
test.read_point: After the first 10 to 20 customers go through the manual version

title: Fix the base effort problem before launching any delight play
hypothesis: If we give customers the fastest refund, replacement or exchange before any gift or surprise, then we avoid the finding that delight after a slow fix gives negligible loyalty gain, and we protect the wild bet program's own results.

signal.check: A wild bet is being planned while support tickets show channel switching, repeated explanations or long waits on returns, cancellations or broken items.

expected_effect.size: no lift figure given; a 97,000+ interaction study found delight after an unresolved failure adds only a negligible loyalty gain

risk.note: A support-process fix; low risk, but skipping it wastes the wild bet budget.

prerequisites: Support tool export of tickets and resolution times
steps: Walk the return, cancellation and broken-item support paths as a customer would.
Record where channel switching, repeated explanations or long waits happen.
Send the fix list to the support and operations team before any wild bet launches.
Do not launch a wild bet on this base until the owner accepts the fix is done or scheduled.

test.method: Re-walk the same 3 paths after fixes ship.
test.measure: Customer Effort Score, first-contact resolution, resolution time
test.read_point: Before any wild bet launch, then re-checked quarterly

title: Build a weekly-refreshed exclusion list of customers with an unresolved failure
hypothesis: If we refresh a list every week of customers with an open or recently closed service failure, then no wild bet or gift ever reaches someone still upset about a late, broken or billing problem.

signal.check: No standing list exists of customers who had a service failure in the last 7 days, and delight sends are not checked against one.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a rate, this is a process control

risk.note: An internal list; no customer sees it directly.

prerequisites: Support tool export with ticket status and dates
steps: Pull customers with a failure (late, broken, billing) opened or closed in the last 7 days.
Refresh this list every week before any delight send goes out.
Cross-check every planned gift, note or drop invite cohort against the list before sending.
Attach the list as a required item on every approval request.

test.method: Audit a sample of sent delight touches against the exclusion list dates.
test.measure: Number of sends that reached an excluded customer

title: Audit CES, first-contact resolution and resolution time before any wild bet
hypothesis: If we pull Customer Effort Score, first-contact resolution, resolution time, transfers per ticket and contacts per order before running any wild bet, then we have a real baseline instead of guessing whether the base is ready for delight.

signal.check: No one can quote current CES, first-contact resolution rate or average resolution time from the support tool.

expected_effect.size: no source gives a pass mark; the owner sets the bar from this baseline

risk.note: A read of existing support data.

prerequisites: Support tool export
steps: Pull CES, first-contact resolution, resolution time, transfers per ticket and contacts per order.
Tag each touchpoint type as operational support or a brand-elevation moment.
Present the baseline to the owner and get a written accept or a fix list.
Re-pull the same numbers after any fix before launching wild bets.

test.method: Compare the baseline against the owner's accepted bar.
test.read_point: Before Stage 1 of the wild bets rollout, then quarterly

title: Compare measured resolution time to customer-reported effort to catch handoffs
hypothesis: If we compare the clock time to resolve a ticket against how effortful the customer says it felt, then a gap tells us handoffs or repeats are hurting even when the timer looks fine.

signal.check: Resolution time looks fast on paper but customers still describe support as frustrating or repetitive.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a target gap size

risk.note: A measurement comparison, not a customer-facing change.

prerequisites: Resolution time data and a way to ask customers about perceived effort
steps: Pull the measured resolution time for a sample of recent tickets.
Ask the same customers a short effort question (how easy was this to resolve).
Flag tickets where perceived effort is high despite a fast measured time.
Investigate those for transfers, repeated explanations or unclear replies.

test.method: Track the gap between measured and perceived effort over time.

title: Split support tickets into fast operational fixes vs relationship-building touches
hypothesis: If we tag tickets as operational support (measured on CES, resolution time) or brand elevation (measured on LTV, referral, repurchase) and never mix the two, then a returns ticket never gets mistaken for a loyalty win.

signal.check: Support metrics and relationship metrics are reported together or a returns fix is being counted as a delight win.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a reporting discipline, no source gives a rate

risk.note: A reporting change only.

prerequisites: A tagging field in the support tool for touchpoint type
steps: Tag every support touchpoint type as Operational Support or Brand Elevation.
For Operational Support, report only CES, first-contact resolution and resolution time.
For Brand Elevation, report only LTV, earned media value, NPS and repurchase rate.
Never let one category's metric stand in for the other in a readout.

test.method: Review readouts for mixed metrics after the split is in place.
test.measure: Whether operational and relationship metrics stay on separate lines

title: Follow the staged rollout order and pass each gate before the next
hypothesis: If we run the base-effort audit, then cheap manual touches, then a VIP tier, then referral and drops, then one big stunt, in that order, then cost and risk stay low while each stage proves itself before the next spend.

signal.check: The team wants to jump to a drop, stunt or referral program before the base-effort audit or the first cheap touches have run.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a sequencing rule, no case number

risk.note: A planning order; skipping a stage raises risk but this check itself is free.

prerequisites: Stage 0 base-effort audit done or scheduled
steps: Confirm Stage 0 (base-effort audit) is done and accepted.
Run Stage 1: a handwritten note or founder video, and a keep-it refund pilot, each with its own control.
Only after a pass, move to Stage 2 (VIP tier), then Stage 3 (referral and drops), then Stage 4 (one stunt a year).
Do not skip a stage without the owner's explicit decision.

test.method: Check each stage's pass mark before approving the next stage's budget.
test.measure: repeat_rate_90d or the stage's named pass mark
test.read_point: At each stage's planned review window (1 month, 90 days, 6 months)

title: Adjust the wild bet plan to margin, product test results and brand voice
hypothesis: If we delay lifetime warranties on thin margins, skip proof-in-the-box when the product does not win a head-to-head test, and skip punk stunts for a serious voice, then the wild bets plan fits this specific brand instead of copying a generic playbook.

signal.check: The default quarterly plan (warranty, proof kit, or a stunt) has not been checked against this brand's margin, product test results or voice.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a fit check, not a measured lift

risk.note: A planning adjustment, made before any spend.

prerequisites: Gross margin by SKU
A brand voice statement
steps: Check gross margin by SKU before proposing a lifetime warranty or price lock.
Run the proof-in-the-box test against a rival privately before ever proposing it publicly.
Check brand voice before proposing any stunt.
Adjust or drop any default-plan item that fails these checks.

test.method: Review the quarterly plan against margin, product-test and voice data before approval.

title: Size and fix a high cash-on-delivery or return-to-origin rate before any delight play
hypothesis: If we measure and fix a high cash-on-delivery share or return-to-origin rate as a base-effort problem, then we remove a hidden cost drag before spending on any wild bet, which a delight play cannot fix.
does_not_apply_when: Cash-on-delivery and return-to-origin are already low and stable

signal.check: Cash-on-delivery share or return-to-origin rate is high and has never been sized or addressed.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: A measurement and fix step against existing operations data.

prerequisites: Order data with payment method and return-to-origin flag
steps: Pull the current cash-on-delivery share and return-to-origin rate.
If either is high, treat it as a Stage 0 fix, not a wild bet target.
Identify the top drivers (address quality, prepaid incentive gaps, fulfilment delays).
Fix the top driver before proposing any wild bet on this cohort.

test.method: Track cash-on-delivery share and return-to-origin rate before and after the fix.

title: Never launch a wild bet without a written 8-field bound
hypothesis: If every wild bet has a written hypothesis, cohort, budget cap, metric, control, duration, stop rule and registry entry before launch, then a human can approve or reject it in one pass and the result can actually be judged later.

signal.check: A wild bet is about to launch, including a 'free' one like a founder video, with any of the 8 bound fields blank or marked TBD.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a governance rule, not a measured lift

risk.note: A documentation requirement before launch.

prerequisites: Brand voice, cash cap and labor hours known
steps: Write the hypothesis as: if we run [play] for [cohort], then [metric] rises vs control by [amount] within [duration].
Define the cohort: who, how many, how ranked, and the exclusions.
Set the budget cap in cash (pieces times cost plus fees plus gifts plus refund exposure) and labor hours.
Set the metric, the control, the duration and review date, the stop rule, and the registry entry id.
Do not submit the approval request until every field is filled with no TBD.

test.method: Checklist review of the bound before the approval request is sent.

title: Draw a randomized control holdout before treating anyone
hypothesis: If we draw a randomized holdout from the same eligible cohort before the treatment list is final, then the readout can actually show whether the play caused the lift instead of just describing who got treated.

signal.check: A wild bet is about to send with no control group, or the 'control' is just the customers who happened to be skipped.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a design rule, no case gives a number

risk.note: A list-splitting step before any send.

prerequisites: A ranked, filtered eligible list for the play
steps: Build the full eligible list for the play after exclusions are applied.
Randomly split off a holdout before anyone is treated, timestamped.
Treat the rest; never let the control group receive the play.
Compare treated vs control at the review date.

test.method: Compare treated vs control on the play's metric at the review date.
test.measure: repeat_rate_90d or the play's named metric
test.read_point: At the play's planned review date

title: Run only one wild bet per cohort per test window
hypothesis: If only one play touches a given cohort in a given test window, then a lift or a miss can be attributed to that one play instead of a bundle of overlapping changes.

signal.check: The same customer segment is scheduled to receive two or more wild bet plays in the same window under one shared benchmark.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a design rule to keep results readable

risk.note: A scheduling check before launch.

prerequisites: A shared calendar of planned cohorts and windows
steps: List every planned play and its cohort and window.
Check for any cohort scheduled to receive more than one play at once.
Split overlapping plays into separate cohorts and controls, or stagger the windows.
Confirm no overlap before sending the approval request.

test.method: Review the shared calendar before each new bet is approved.

title: Cap cohort size and send frequency at what the team can sustain by hand
hypothesis: If we shrink a manual cohort or slow the sending frequency to what the team can actually keep up by hand, then quality per touch stays high instead of degrading as volume grows.

signal.check: A manual play's cohort size or send frequency was set by ambition rather than by counting the team's real hours.

expected_effect.size: one case caps programmatic mail at 1 mailing per customer per 30 days; no ecommerce-wide figure

risk.note: A sizing decision, made before launch.

prerequisites: Labor hours available for manual touches
steps: Count the real hours the team has for this manual play per week.
Divide by the time each touch takes to get a sustainable cohort size or send rate.
Shrink the planned cohort or slow the cadence to match, rather than hiring or rushing.
Revisit the cap only after the play proves it is worth the added labor.

test.method: Track missed or rushed touches against the cap.

title: Never count an unverified hedge or earned-media estimate as funding
hypothesis: If we fund the maximum possible liability of a promotion or promise in cash, and treat any hedge or earned-media estimate as a bonus rather than funding, then the store cannot be caught unable to pay out a promise it made.

signal.check: A promotion's budget relies on a prediction-market hedge, expected virality, or an earned-media estimate to cover its worst-case cost.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no case number, this is a funding rule

risk.note: Skipping this check can leave a real, unfunded liability if a promotion pays out.

prerequisites: Maximum liability calculation for the promotion
steps: Calculate the maximum possible payout if every eligible order qualifies.
Confirm that amount is funded in cash on hand, not by a hedge or a virality assumption.
If a hedge exists, record its stake, payout and settlement date as a bonus, never as the funding line.
Track earned media on its own separate line, never as revenue or funding.

test.method: Audit the funding line against the maximum liability before launch.

title: Write a specific stop rule before every wild bet launches
hypothesis: If every bet's stop rule names a number or event (cap hit, no lift at review, fraud signal, backlash, return rate rising) instead of a vague 'if it doesn't work', then the team can decide to stop without a debate in the moment.

signal.check: A bet's stop rule reads as a vague phrase instead of a specific number or event.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a governance rule, no case number

risk.note: A planning step, not a live change.

prerequisites: The bet's cap, control and metric already set
steps: List the ways this specific play could go wrong: cap hit, no lift at review, fraud signal, refunds rising, backlash, checkout conversion dropping.
Pick the ones that apply to this play and write them as specific numbers or events.
Attach the stop rule to the bound before the approval request.
Check whether the stop rule fired at the readout, and record it either way.

test.method: Check stop-rule status at every readout.

title: Run a legal and consent review before any bet that promises, mails, texts or gates access
hypothesis: If a legal, consent and platform review runs before any bet that promises, refunds, mails, texts, uses third-party data, gates access, runs a contest or pays customers, then the brand avoids a legal or platform problem it did not see coming.

signal.check: A bet involves a promise, physical mail, SMS, third-party data, gated access, a contest or a customer payment, and no legal or platform review has happened yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives legal steps, this is a process gate

risk.note: Skipping this can create real legal or platform exposure; running it is low-risk.

prerequisites: Knowledge of the selling market's consumer protection, contest, warranty and privacy rules
steps: List every element of the bet that touches promises, mail, SMS, third-party data, gating, contests or payments.
Check consumer protection, contest and promotion, warranty, SMS consent, and privacy rules for the selling market.
Get sign-off with a named owner and status for each item.
Attach the review status to the approval request before launch.

test.method: Checklist review before approval; re-check when entering a new market.
test.read_point: Before every approval request, and every quarter for standing programs

title: Judge every wild bet at its planned review date, not on a viral spike or quiet week
hypothesis: If we read out a wild bet only at its planned review date, not early on a viral moment or late after a quiet week, then the decision reflects the real slower build most non-paid plays need instead of a lucky or unlucky snapshot.
does_not_apply_when: A transactional play (a flash sale, a drop) that is meant to be read in its own short window

signal.check: A team wants to call a bet a win or a loss before its planned review date, based on an early spike or a quiet first week.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources describe non-paid growth as a slower, more profitable build, no figure given

risk.note: A patience rule, not a live change.

prerequisites: A review date already set in the bound
steps: Set the review date in the bound before launch and do not move it based on early results.
If a viral spike happens, log it as a signal, not the decision.
If the first weeks look quiet, wait for the planned date rather than killing the play early.
Read out and decide only at the planned date, unless the stop rule fires first.

test.method: Compare the readout date actually used against the planned date.

title: Never treat another brand's reported lift as a benchmark; test it on this store's own cohort
hypothesis: If a reported repeat-purchase lift, ROAS or conversion figure from another brand is treated as an idea to test rather than a target this store must hit, then plans do not get built on numbers with no sample size, duration or margin behind them.

signal.check: A plan or pitch quotes another brand's case result (a vendor case, a founder claim) as the expected outcome for this store.

expected_effect.size: unknown; all 3 sources' own methodology sections say the same thing

risk.note: A labeling and expectation-setting discipline.

prerequisites: None
steps: Whenever a case number is quoted in a brief, label it with its source and the words reported, unaudited.
Never use it as the target lift in a hypothesis.
Let the human set the minimum lift the store actually wants to see.
Test the idea on this store's own cohort and compare against this store's own control.

test.method: Review bet briefs for unlabeled case numbers before approval.

title: Judge wild bets on relationship metrics and incremental contribution, not vanity attention
hypothesis: If the readout reports incremental contribution after all program costs as the decision line, with relationship metrics like repeat rate and referral share, then the team stops or scales a bet on real return instead of on likes and shares.

signal.check: A past bet's readout used reach, likes or traffic as the reason to double down, with no contribution or repeat-rate number attached.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a number, this is a measurement discipline

risk.note: A reporting change; the risk sits in the bet, not this rule.

prerequisites: Cost tracking for the bet (cash and labor) and a control group
steps: Pull treated and control outcomes at the review date.
Compute incremental contribution after all program costs, in code or a spreadsheet, not by hand.
Report it as the decision line, and word-of-mouth, referral, NPS or UGC as a separate signal line.
Decide double down, keep, change one variable, or kill, based on the decision line.

test.method: Compute both lines at every readout and keep them on separate rows.

title: Track earned media and UGC as a signal line, never as revenue
hypothesis: If earned media value, UGC and shares are tracked on their own line and never added into the revenue or contribution line, then a viral moment cannot make a losing bet look like a win on paper.

signal.check: A readout or business case adds an earned-media estimate into the revenue or return figure.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a method to value coverage against spend

risk.note: A reporting separation, no live change.

prerequisites: A way to track mentions, shares and coverage separately from sales
steps: Log mentions, shares, UGC volume and any press coverage separately from order data.
Never sum an earned-media estimate into the contribution or revenue figure.
Present it as a labeled signal line next to, not inside, the decision line.
Get the owner to approve the valuation method before quoting an earned-media number publicly.

test.method: Audit readouts for earned media mixed into revenue.

title: Control for prior spend before crediting a wild bet for an engaged-customer gap
hypothesis: If we control for prior spend before comparing content-engaged customers to non-engaged ones, then a real gap survives the check, while a fake one (people who already bought more) disappears instead of being credited to the content.

signal.check: A comparison of engaged vs non-engaged customer LTV is being used to justify a wild bet, with no check for whether engaged customers already spent more before engaging.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source's 3.5x LTV figure is confounded by self-selection and not usable as-is

risk.note: An analysis step against existing data.

prerequisites: Customer-level engagement data joined to order history
steps: Pull LTV for content-engaged and non-engaged customers.
Segment both groups by prior spend before the engagement started.
Compare LTV again within matched prior-spend bands.
If the gap shrinks or disappears, do not claim the content caused it.

test.method: Compare the raw gap to the prior-spend-controlled gap.
test.read_point: Before crediting any content or engagement program with a lift

title: Judge a paid loyalty tier on spend and retention lift, not on enrollment count
hypothesis: If a paid loyalty tier is judged on spend and retention lift versus comparable non-members, not on how many people signed up, then the tier's real value is visible instead of hidden behind a headcount number.

signal.check: A paid loyalty tier's success is being reported as a signup count with no comparison to non-member spend or retention.

expected_effect.size: a reported figure (via a blog, no method given): paid members up to 60% more likely to increase spend, twice the rate of free-program members

risk.note: A measurement change, not a live tier change.

prerequisites: A comparable group of non-members matched on prior spend
steps: Pull spend and retention for paid tier members after enrollment.
Build a matched comparison group of non-members with similar prior spend.
Compare spend and retention lift, not signup counts, as the success metric.
Report the matched comparison, noting it is not a randomized control.

test.method: Compare member vs matched non-member spend and retention at a set interval.

title: Put a trackable response device on every physical piece sent to a customer
hypothesis: If every note, letter, insert or mail piece carries a QR code, unique URL or unique discount code, then the piece's response can actually be read instead of guessed.

signal.check: A physical piece (note, letter, insert, mailer) is planned with no way to trace whether the recipient responded.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a design requirement, no lift figure

risk.note: A design addition to the piece before printing or sending.

prerequisites: A way to generate unique codes, URLs or QR codes per recipient or per batch
steps: Decide the device: QR code, unique URL, unique or private discount code, or a tear-off referral insert.
Generate the device per recipient or per control-vs-treated batch.
Add it clearly to the piece before it goes out.
Track scans, code use or visits back to the campaign.

test.method: Track device use rate against the cohort size.

title: Report the source's reported effect next to this store's own measured effect
hypothesis: If every deliverable shows the source's case figure, labeled with its origin, right next to this store's own control comparison, then no one confuses someone else's vendor case with this brand's real result.

signal.check: A deliverable states an expected effect without saying whether it is a case example or this store's own measured number.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a reporting format rule, no case number

risk.note: A formatting rule for deliverables.

prerequisites: None
steps: In the bet brief, quote the source's case figure with its label (vendor case, founder claim, blog, press).
Add a separate column or line for this store's own measured control comparison once available.
Never merge the two into one number.
Use this format in every bet brief, readout and registry entry.

test.method: Review deliverables for merged or unlabeled figures.

title: Start costly touches at the smallest proven cohort and widen only after a passed gate
hypothesis: If costly personal touches start at 10 to 50 customers by hand, expand to 200 only after a passed control read, and reach the top 1% only as a standing tier after Stage 2, then spend grows only where it has already proven a lift.

signal.check: A costly touch program is being sized directly at the top 1% or the full customer list with no smaller proof step first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the claim that the top 1% drives most revenue is asserted in the source, not shown, and must be measured on this store

risk.note: A sizing ladder, not a live send by itself.

prerequisites: Customer list ranked by lifetime spend
Revenue share of top 1%, top 5%, top 50 and top 200 measured
steps: Measure the actual revenue share of the top 1%, 5%, 50 and 200 customers; do not assume it.
Start the touch at 10 to 50 customers by hand, with a control.
Expand to 200 only if repeat or 90-day reorder beats control.
Treat the top 1% as a standing tier only after the expanded cohort also passes.

test.method: Compare repeat and reorder rate of each cohort stage vs its control before widening.
test.read_point: At each stage's planned review date

title: Reserve costly personal touches for repeat buyers with shown affinity
hypothesis: If handwritten notes, artifacts and other costly personal touches go only to repeat buyers who have already shown affinity, not first-time buyers, then the spend goes where the relationship already exists to build on.
does_not_apply_when: Cheap automated mail or a low-cost first-order insert can still target new customers, under its own control

signal.check: A costly handwritten or artifact touch is planned for a customer with only one order and no shown affinity.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no case gives a lift figure for this targeting rule alone

risk.note: A targeting filter before sending.

prerequisites: Order history with repeat-purchase flag
steps: Filter the planned cohort to repeat buyers with at least one prior repeat purchase.
For costly touches (above the cents-to-a-few-dollars insert range), require the repeat-buyer filter.
Route new-customer touches to cheap, automated plays with their own control instead.
Review the filter whenever a new costly touch is proposed.

test.method: Compare repeat and reorder rate of the filtered cohort vs a first-time-buyer control group.

title: Only send emotional gifts in categories with a real emotional hook
hypothesis: If a gift or emotional art play only runs in categories with a real hook (pet, home, car, baby, hobby), then the gift has something to touch, instead of landing in a purely functional category where it gets no shares.
does_not_apply_when: A purely functional category with no emotional hook (the source names this as getting no shares)

signal.check: A gift or custom-art play is planned for a category with no clear emotional connection point.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources name the hook requirement, not a rate

risk.note: A fit check before designing the gift.

prerequisites: None
steps: Name the category's emotional hook, if any (pet, home, car, baby, hobby, a life event).
If no real hook exists, do not run the emotional gift or art play here.
If a hook exists, design the gift or art to touch it directly, not generically.
Track posts, shares and repeat purchase from recipients vs non-recipients.

test.method: Compare share and repeat rate of gift recipients vs a non-recipient control.

title: Build direct mail segments from lifecycle signals, not the whole list
hypothesis: If programmatic mail segments are built from VIPs, repeat buyers, high-value cart abandoners, lapsed buyers, new members and high-consideration browsers, then the cost of physical mail goes only where the response is more likely.

signal.check: A direct mail plan targets the entire customer list rather than a lifecycle-based segment.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the compiler's lapsed window (6 to 12 months) and second-purchase window (30 to 60 days) are advice, not measured for this brand

risk.note: A targeting step for an otherwise standard mail program.

prerequisites: A mail vendor available in the brand's country
Address data quality checked
steps: List the lifecycle segments: VIPs, repeat buyers, high-value cart abandoners, lapsed buyers, new members, high-consideration browsers.
Find this brand's own repurchase interval instead of copying a compiler's window.
Pick the segment with the most volume and the highest cart value to start.
Test timing as a variable within that segment rather than assuming a fixed window.

test.method: A/B test the segment and timing against an email-only and a no-contact control.
test.read_point: One wave plus the repurchase window

title: Reserve flash sales for loyalty segments only, never the full list
hypothesis: If a flash sale goes only to a loyalty segment with a clear urgency cue, then it reads as a reward for that segment instead of a blanket discount that erodes brand value for everyone else.
does_not_apply_when: Segment data is not clean enough to prevent the offer from leaking to the full list

signal.check: A flash sale is planned to go to the entire subscriber or customer list rather than a defined loyalty segment.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source names a high-visibility urgency cue example (a bright banner reading Expires Tomorrow), no lift figure given

risk.note: A leaked or repeated flash sale can train discount dependency and erode brand value.

prerequisites: Clean loyalty segment data with no leak points
steps: Define the loyalty segment eligible for the flash sale.
Add a clear, high-visibility urgency cue (a countdown or an explicit expiry banner).
Send only to the segment; check for leak points (shared codes, public links).
Measure conversion and brand perception together, and watch for leakage into the full list.

test.method: Track conversion, discount rate and any leak signals after each flash sale.
test.read_point: Immediately after the sale window closes

title: Build separate stage gates and cohort sizes for single-hero-SKU stores vs catalogues
hypothesis: If a single-hero-SKU store runs a waitlist- or launch-based version of the top-50, top-200 and top-1% stages instead of copying a catalogue store's repeat-purchase cohorts, then the stage gates actually fit how that store's customers buy.
does_not_apply_when: A catalogue store with a large, frequently repurchasing customer base, where the standard cohort ladder already fits

signal.check: A single-hero-SKU store is trying to build a top-50 or top-200 repeat-purchase cohort the same way a catalogue business would, and the numbers do not fill.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: A planning adaptation, not a live change.

prerequisites: Repeat-purchase rate and order history for the store's actual product mix
steps: Check whether the store's repeat-purchase base can fill a top-50 or top-200 cohort in a reasonable time.
If not, build a waitlist- or launch-based version of the same stage instead (an early-access list, a drop waitlist).
Size cohorts to the store's real order volume, not a catalogue store's numbers.
Re-check as the store's repeat base grows.

test.method: Compare cohort fill time for the standard vs the waitlist-based version.

title: Send a handwritten note or 60-second founder video to the top cohort, with a control
hypothesis: If we send a handwritten note referencing a specific past purchase, or a short founder video, to the top 10 to 50 customers with a control group, then repeat-purchase and 90-day reorder rate can be tested against a real baseline.

signal.check: The top customers by lifetime spend have never received a personal, non-automated touch from the founder or team.

expected_effect.size: no case gives a lift; sources say to expand the touch only if repeat-purchase rate rises vs control

risk.note: A note or video cannot be recalled once sent; low risk since it is not a public claim.

prerequisites: Customer list ranked by lifetime spend
Exclusion list applied
Founder or team hours available
steps: Rank customers by lifetime spend; take the top 50, or top 10 if hours are tight.
Remove anyone in a failure state using the exclusion list.
Randomly hold out a control from the same ranked list before writing anything.
Write each note referencing a real past purchase, or record a short founder video.
Pick a no-code (gratitude only) or a private-code version and record the choice.
Log recipients, send dates and control ids, and compare at the review date.

test.method: Compare repeat-purchase rate and 90-day reorder rate, treated vs control.
test.read_point: 90 days after sends, with referrals logged separately

title: Once a year, have executives handwrite thank-you notes to the top 1% of repeat buyers with no code
hypothesis: If executives handwrite a once-a-year note to the top 1% of repeat buyers naming their past purchases, with no discount code, then it reads as gratitude rather than a direct-response campaign, and repeat rate can still be read against a control.

signal.check: No annual, purely gratitude-based touch exists for the very top repeat-buyer cohort.

expected_effect.size: no case number in any source

risk.note: A handwritten letter cannot be recalled; low risk since it carries no public claim.

prerequisites: Top 1% of repeat buyers list
Executive hours capped at what can be handwritten
steps: Once a year, pull the top 1% of repeat buyers, capped at what the executive team can actually handwrite.
Have each letter name the buyer's specific past purchases.
Include no discount code; gratitude only.
Pick a random send date away from holidays and anniversaries.
Draw a control before writing and budget the whole activity as a fixed small cost, not a campaign.

test.method: Compare repeat-purchase rate at the repurchase interval, treated vs control.
test.read_point: At the store's repurchase interval after sends

title: Send an annual or anniversary letter to repeat buyers with a private code as the response device
hypothesis: If the annual or anniversary letter to repeat buyers carries a private offer code or a tear-off referral insert, then the store can measure its response instead of treating it as pure, unmeasured gratitude.
does_not_apply_when: The owner wants the annual letter to stay pure gratitude with no measurement; do not mix a code into that version

signal.check: An annual or anniversary letter is planned with no way to measure whether it drove a purchase or referral.

expected_effect.size: cost about $1 to $5 per piece (vendor estimate); no redemption or lift figure given

risk.note: A letter cannot be recalled once sent.

prerequisites: Repeat buyer list
A private code or referral insert generator
steps: Pick repeat buyers for the annual or anniversary letter cohort.
Add a private offer code or a perforated tear-off referral insert as the response device.
Keep the send date off holidays and purchase anniversaries where the play is meant as a surprise.
Measure code redemption and repeat rate against a randomized control.

test.method: Track code redemptions and repeat rate, treated vs control.

title: Never send printed notes made to look handwritten
hypothesis: If personal notes are genuinely handwritten instead of printed to look handwritten, then customers do not feel tricked, which a printed imitation risks once noticed.

signal.check: A handwriting service or printed font is being considered to fake a handwritten look at scale.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source states this as a feel check, no measured figure

risk.note: A sourcing decision for the note itself.

prerequisites: None
steps: Decide whether the note will be truly hand-written or produced at scale.
If scale is needed, use a genuine handwriting service only once volume justifies it, and disclose internally how it works.
Never present a printed, font-based imitation as handwritten.
Spot-check a sample of sent notes for authenticity before scaling further.

test.method: Spot-check a sample of notes against the stated method.
test.read_point: Before and during any scaling of the note program

title: Never send costly personal mail to the whole customer list
hypothesis: If costly personal mail (notes, letters, art) is capped to a proven repeat-buyer segment instead of the whole list, then cost stays proportional to expected return instead of scaling with list size alone.

signal.check: A costly mail or note program is being planned for the entire customer list rather than a defined segment.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a cost-control rule, no case figure

risk.note: A budgeting check before the mail run.

prerequisites: A defined proven-repeat-buyer segment
steps: Define the proven repeat-buyer segment eligible for costly personal mail.
Check the planned cohort against the full customer list count.
If the cohort is the whole list, shrink it to the proven segment before sending.
Revisit the segment size only after a passed control read.

test.method: Compare planned cohort size to total list size before every mail run.

title: Forward every post-purchase and shipping email to the founder for a month
hypothesis: If the founder personally reads and replies to every post-purchase, shipping and return email for one month while volume is low, then real checkout and delivery pain points surface faster than any survey would find them.
does_not_apply_when: Support volume is too high for the founder to reply within the service SLA

signal.check: Support volume is still low, and the founder has never personally read a month of post-purchase and shipping emails.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source claims more is learned in 30 days than a year of surveys, a claim with no data

risk.note: Time-bound to one month while volume is low; can stop any time.

prerequisites: Support volume low enough to stay within the service SLA
steps: Set up forwarding of every post-purchase, shipping and return email to the founder for one month.
Have the founder reply personally within the normal service SLA.
Log themes and pain points weekly.
Route the fix list to the operations team before any wild bet launches.

test.method: Review the weekly theme log for recurring pain points.
test.read_point: Weekly during the month, then a summary at month end

title: Map the journey of 20 real customers and mark where a human touch fits
hypothesis: If we write out every step 20 real customers take from discovery to repeat purchase, and mark where a manual human touch fits, then the wild bets plan targets real moments instead of guessing where personal attention matters.

signal.check: No one has written out the actual step-by-step journey of real customers from discovery to post-purchase.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a planning exercise, no measured figure

risk.note: An internal exercise, not a live change.

prerequisites: Access to order and support data for 20 real customers
steps: Pick 20 real customers spanning discovery, purchase and repeat behavior.
Write every touchpoint from ad or search to PDP, cart, checkout, and repeat purchase.
Ask: if these were the only 20 customers, what would make each feel like the only one?
Mark where a manual, human touch fits and feed it into the note, gift, insert or frontline budget plays.

test.method: Not tested on its own; feeds the design of resulting plays.
test.read_point: Reviewed once per quarter as the customer base grows

title: Use the local messaging channel customers already use for notes and drop alerts
hypothesis: If notes, drop alerts and reminders go out on WhatsApp or whichever local channel customers actually use to talk, instead of or alongside email and mail, then messages get seen where customers already are.

signal.check: Notes, drop alerts or reminders are only sent by email or mail, while customers mostly talk to the brand through WhatsApp or another local channel.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: A channel choice; requires consent for the channel used.

prerequisites: Consent to message on the local channel
A way to send from it (business account or tool)
steps: Confirm which channel customers actually respond on (WhatsApp or similar).
Get consent to message customers on that channel where required.
Route founder notes, drop alerts and reminders through it, alongside or instead of email and mail.
Compare open and response rate against the email or mail version.

test.method: Compare response rate between the local channel and email or mail for the same message.
test.read_point: After the first batch of sends

title: Trigger a physical mail piece from the same lifecycle signal that fires an email
hypothesis: If a mail vendor is connected to the email platform so the same event fires both, then the mail piece can be tested against an email-only control from the same trigger instead of a different, uncontrolled moment.

signal.check: A direct mail idea exists with no plan to connect it to the same trigger that fires the matching lifecycle email.

expected_effect.size: vendor cases report a range from about 7.5% redemption to 22x reported incremental ROAS; unaudited and undefined in most cases

risk.note: Turning off the trigger stops future mail; printed pieces already sent are sunk.

prerequisites: A mail vendor available in the brand's country
ESP integration capability
steps: Map lifecycle journeys: welcome, abandoned cart, browse, post-purchase, second purchase, birthday, win-back.
Pick the moment with the most volume and highest cart value for a high-value segment.
Connect the mail vendor to the ESP so the same event fires mail and email.
Confirm the integration fires correctly on a test event before going live.

test.method: Run the mail-plus-email group against an email-only control and a no-contact holdout.
test.read_point: One wave plus the repurchase window

title: Personalize each mail piece with the exact abandoned or recommended product
hypothesis: If each mail piece shows the exact abandoned or recommended product and tailors the offer by cohort, then the piece feels relevant to that customer instead of generic, which vendor cases link to higher conversion.

signal.check: A planned mail piece uses generic creative with no per-customer product personalization.

expected_effect.size: vendor cases report 38.81% higher conversions and 22% more conversions from personalized mail; unaudited

risk.note: A creative and data-feed decision within an otherwise standard mail program.

prerequisites: Product-level data feed to the mail vendor
A cohort-specific offer structure
steps: Pull the exact abandoned or recommended product per customer.
Feed it to the mail vendor's personalization template.
Tailor the offer by cohort (VIP, lapsed, new member) rather than using one flat offer.
Compare personalized vs generic creative in an A/B test.

test.method: A/B test personalized vs generic mail creative.

title: Run two controls on any direct mail test: email-only and no-contact
hypothesis: If a mail test splits customers into mail-plus-email, email-only and a randomized no-contact holdout, then the readout can separate mail's lift over email from whether mail is incremental at all.

signal.check: A mail test is planned with only a mail-vs-no-mail split, unable to separate mail's own lift from the email that runs alongside it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a design rule, not a lift figure

risk.note: A test design step before the mail run.

prerequisites: A large enough eligible pool to split 3 ways
steps: Split eligible customers 3 ways before sending: mail plus email, email only, no contact.
Randomize the split so it is not a convenience grouping.
Run the mail piece to the treated group only.
Compare all 3 groups at the review date to see both mail's lift over email and mail's own incrementality.

test.method: Compare conversion and revenue across the 3 groups.
test.read_point: One wave plus the repurchase window

title: Match mail format and paper stock to brand values
hypothesis: If the paper stock and format of a mail piece match the brand's values (recycled paper for a sustainability brand, premium stock for a luxury one), then the physical object itself reinforces the brand instead of contradicting it.

signal.check: A mail piece's paper stock or format has not been checked against the brand's stated values or positioning.

expected_effect.size: a vendor case credits paper stock and personalization detail with up to 13.6% conversion; the detail is a claim, not a shown test

risk.note: A material choice before printing.

prerequisites: A brand values or positioning statement
steps: Check the brand's stated values (sustainability, luxury, playful, minimal).
Pick a paper stock and print format that matches, not the vendor's cheapest default.
Confirm the format still fits the budget cap.
Review recipient feedback or complaints about the physical piece.

test.method: Compare response between the matched format and any prior mismatched format, where available.

title: Vet third-party address or spend data before targeting with it
hypothesis: If we ask exactly how a third-party address or spend-data segment was obtained and confirm it is legal to use before targeting with it, then a mail or ad program does not build on data the brand cannot legally use.

signal.check: A vendor or partner offers a third-party address or spend-data segment (competitor customers, 'anonymized insights') with no documentation of how it was obtained.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no result given for the source's case (a competitor-customer mail program), this is a risk check

risk.note: Using improperly sourced third-party data can create real privacy and legal exposure.

prerequisites: Local privacy law reference (GDPR, India DPDP, or equivalent)
steps: Ask the data provider exactly how the segment and addresses were obtained.
Confirm the specific use case (this campaign, this audience) is covered by their terms.
Check local privacy rules (GDPR, India DPDP or equivalent) before using address-based targeting.
Get written confirmation before the data is used, not after.

test.method: Not a performance test; a compliance gate.
test.read_point: Before any third-party data is used

title: Feed mail response signals back into email and retargeting follow-ups
hypothesis: If a QR scan or code use from a mail piece triggers a digital follow-up email or retargeting ad, then the mail spend gets a second chance to convert instead of ending at the mailbox.

signal.check: Mail response signals (scans, code redemptions) are tracked but nothing digital happens afterward.

expected_effect.size: a vendor case reports an 88% open rate on the digital follow-up email to 12,000 contacts; unaudited

risk.note: An automation wiring step.

prerequisites: Mail vendor and ESP integration already in place
steps: Identify the response signals available from the mail vendor (scans, code use).
Wire those signals to trigger a specific follow-up email or retargeting segment.
Test the follow-up message against a version with no follow-up.
Track conversion from the follow-up separately from the original mail piece.

test.method: Compare conversion for responders who got the follow-up vs those who did not.
test.read_point: Within the follow-up campaign's own window

title: Check direct mail vendor coverage in the brand's country before planning a program
hypothesis: If we confirm a direct mail vendor actually operates and can match addresses in this brand's country before planning a program, then the plan does not stall on a vendor that only covers the EU, UK or US.

signal.check: A direct mail program is being planned before checking whether any named vendor covers the brand's actual country.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named vendors in the source are EU, UK and US only, India coverage unconfirmed

risk.note: A research step before committing budget.

prerequisites: None
steps: List candidate mail vendors and check their stated country coverage.
Confirm identity-match capability and pricing for the brand's actual market.
If no vendor covers the market, hold the play and look for local alternatives.
Re-check vendor coverage before every new market's mail plan.

test.method: Not a performance test; a feasibility gate.
test.read_point: Before planning any direct mail program

title: A/B test mail offer, creative, timing and format, and roll winners forward
hypothesis: If direct mail is treated like a digital channel and its offer, creative, timing and format are A/B tested, then later waves can roll the winner forward instead of repeating the same untested piece.

signal.check: The same mail piece has run multiple waves with no variation tested against it.

expected_effect.size: a vendor case reports ROI up 128% from A/B-tested personalized mail; undefined ROI, unaudited

risk.note: A testing process on top of an existing mail program.

prerequisites: A mail program already running with baseline results
steps: Pick one variable to test in the next wave: offer, creative, timing or format.
Split the eligible cohort randomly between the current version and the variant.
Measure conversion for each version.
Roll the winner forward as the new baseline and pick the next variable to test.

test.method: A/B test one variable per wave.
test.read_point: At the end of each wave

title: Send a physical welcome kit to new loyalty or club members
hypothesis: If new loyalty or club members get a physical welcome (a personal note, a small gift, a clear benefits list), then reorder and referral among new members can be tracked against a control instead of assumed.

signal.check: New loyalty or club members get only a digital welcome email, with no physical touch.

expected_effect.size: a vendor case reports 3.4% to 13.6% conversion across 7 countries, a 4x spread; unaudited

risk.note: Fulfilment adds a step to onboarding; test on a subset first.

prerequisites: A packing process that can add an item
A defined benefits list for members
steps: Design the welcome kit: a personal note, a small gift, and a clear list of member benefits.
Randomize by member id: half get the kit, half get the standard digital welcome.
Track reorder and referral for both groups.
Scale the kit only if it beats the standard welcome at the review date.

test.method: Compare reorder and referral, kit vs standard welcome.

title: Send an unbranded, high-quality artifact gift matched to a known preference
hypothesis: If the top repeat-buyer cohort gets a high-quality, practical item with no logo, matched to a preference the customer actually stated, then it reads as a real gift instead of swag, and can build referral and repeat behavior.
does_not_apply_when: No stated preference is on file; do not guess at a gift

signal.check: A gift program is being planned using logo items (t-shirts, mugs, pens) instead of a preference-matched artifact.

expected_effect.size: expect negative direct ROI; judge on UGC, referral and repeat before scaling, no lift figure given

risk.note: A one-time gift; low risk if targeted correctly, wasted cost if the preference is wrong.

prerequisites: Zero-party preference data or support notes on file
Supply of the artifact secured
steps: Confirm a stated preference exists for the recipient from zero-party data or support notes.
Pick a high-quality, practical item with no company branding that matches it.
Rank and select the top 1% repeat-buyer cohort; draw a control first.
Ship with no announcement and no purchase requirement; log recipient, item, cost and date.

test.method: Track posts, shares, referrals and repeat rate vs control.

title: Send surprise gifts on a random date, never a holiday or purchase anniversary
hypothesis: If surprise gifts land on a random date instead of a holiday, birthday or purchase anniversary, then the gift reads as an unearned surprise instead of an expected obligation that competes with other gifts that season.
does_not_apply_when: A triggered birthday letter measured on redemption, run as a lifecycle touch, not a pure surprise

signal.check: A gift or surprise send is scheduled on a holiday, birthday or purchase anniversary.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source measures the effect of timing alone

risk.note: A scheduling choice for an already-planned gift.

prerequisites: A gift program already designed
steps: Pick a random date away from any known holiday, birthday or purchase anniversary for each recipient.
Spread sends across the calendar so none lands in a heavy gifting season.
Keep the annual gratitude letter (if any) as a separate, planned exception.
Track whether recipients treat the gift as a surprise (unprompted thanks) vs an expectation.

test.method: Compare recipient reaction (unprompted mentions, shares) between random-date and occasion-date sends where both exist.

title: Keep every surprise unannounced and stop it if customers start expecting it
hypothesis: If a surprise gift stays unannounced with no purchase requirement, and the program stops the moment customers start expecting or asking for it, then the randomness that makes it work is protected instead of turning into a standard perk.

signal.check: Customers have started asking when their gift is coming, or the gift has become an expected part of ordering.

expected_effect.size: case example: about 1,000 hand-painted gifts a week, unannounced, since 2013 (press reports, company claim)

risk.note: A program rule to monitor and enforce.

prerequisites: A gift program already running
steps: Never announce the gift program publicly or promise it as a benefit.
Watch support tickets and social mentions for signs customers expect or ask for it.
If expectation signals appear, stop or change the program rather than let it become a standard perk.
Keep the reasons behind any stop in the registry entry.

test.method: Monitor support and social mentions for expectation language.

title: Commission cheap custom art tied to a personal artifact for a small weekly set of loyal buyers
hypothesis: If a small weekly set of loyal repeat buyers gets a cheap custom art piece of something the product touches (a pet, a car, a home), unannounced, then shares and repeat purchase can be tracked against non-recipients before scaling.
does_not_apply_when: The category has no emotional hook (pet, home, car, baby, hobby)

signal.check: The category has a real emotional hook and no art or artifact gift program exists yet for loyal repeat buyers.

expected_effect.size: cost estimate $20 to $40 per piece; no lift figure given, expect negative direct ROI and judge on repeat and shares

risk.note: A one-time gift per recipient; secure artist supply before scaling.

prerequisites: Artists or suppliers secured for the expected weekly volume
steps: Pick a personal artifact the product touches for each category (pet, home, car, baby, hobby).
Choose a small weekly set of loyal repeat buyers, drawing a control first.
Commission the custom art piece at roughly $20 to $40 per piece.
Ship unannounced and track posts, shares and repeat purchase vs control before scaling.

test.method: Compare share and repeat rate of recipients vs a matched non-recipient control.

title: Secure enough gift supply before scaling a gift-with-order program
hypothesis: If artist or vendor supply is confirmed for the expected weekly order volume before scaling a gift-with-order program, then gifts never delay shipping or force a scramble for supply mid-program.

signal.check: A gift-with-order or artifact program is being scaled up without a confirmed supply agreement for the expected volume.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a supply-chain precaution, no case figure

risk.note: Scaling without secured supply risks shipping delays across all orders, not just the gift.

prerequisites: A pilot version of the gift program already running at small scale
steps: Estimate expected weekly order volume once the gift program scales.
Line up enough artists or vendors to cover that volume with buffer.
Confirm turnaround time does not add to normal shipping time.
Only then expand the gift program beyond its pilot cohort.

test.method: Track shipping time before and after the gift program scales.
test.read_point: During the first month of scaled volume

title: Judge a signature gift program on UGC, referral and repeat, not on direct ROI
hypothesis: If a signature gift program is judged on UGC, referrals and repeat purchase before scaling, and negative direct ROI is expected, then the program is not killed early for looking unprofitable on a P&L line it was never meant to win.

signal.check: A gift program is being judged purely on direct cost recovery, with no tracking of UGC, referral or repeat behavior.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no ecommerce-specific lift figure, case is a brand claim of loyalty and heavy sharing

risk.note: A measurement framing decision.

prerequisites: A gift program already running with a control group
steps: Set expectations before launch that direct ROI on the gift itself will likely be negative.
Track UGC, referral rate and repeat purchase for recipients vs control.
Report those as the decision line at the review date, not the gift's raw cost recovery.
Scale only if UGC, referral or repeat shows a real lift.

test.method: Compare UGC, referral and repeat rate, recipients vs control.
test.read_point: At the play's planned review date

title: Send inner-circle gifts only with a volunteered preference and no strings attached
hypothesis: If a gift meant for a customer's spouse, child or assistant is only sent when the customer volunteered a relevant preference, delivered through the buyer, with no review or referral obligation attached, then the gesture stays a gift instead of feeling invasive.
does_not_apply_when: The household preference was inferred from unrelated data rather than volunteered directly by the customer

signal.check: A gift for a customer's family member or assistant is planned based on inferred data rather than something the customer stated directly.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source's evidence is a single business-relationship case, not an ecommerce result

risk.note: Inferring family ties from data can feel invasive and cannot be undone once sent.

prerequisites: A volunteered, on-record preference from the customer
steps: Confirm the preference was volunteered by the customer, not inferred from purchase or browsing data.
Deliver any gift through the buyer, not directly to the family member.
Attach no review, referral or purchase obligation to the gift.
Skip the play entirely if no volunteered preference exists.

test.method: Not a performance test; a consent and appropriateness gate.

title: Budget top-cohort gifts as a fixed quarterly cost, not a per-order spend to optimize
hypothesis: If gifts to the top repeat-buyer cohort are budgeted as a fixed quarterly line against gross margin, instead of a per-order cost to squeeze down, then the program is judged on its relationship result instead of being nickel-and-dimed into something cheap and forgettable.

signal.check: A gift program's cost is being tracked and optimized per order rather than as one fixed quarterly line.

expected_effect.size: unknown; an opinion-grade budgeting approach, no measured figure

risk.note: A budgeting framing, not a live customer change.

prerequisites: Gross margin figure to set the quarterly cap against
steps: Set a fixed quarterly cash line for the top-cohort gift program, sized against gross margin.
Do not track or shrink the per-order gift cost as a standalone efficiency metric.
Review the whole line's contribution (repeat, referral) at the quarter's end.
Adjust the fixed line up or down only at the next quarterly plan.

test.method: Review the full quarter's gift line against repeat and referral outcomes.

title: Add a low-cost personal insert to first or VIP orders tied to a tracked action
hypothesis: If a low-cost, personal insert (a sticker, sample or small gift) with a handwritten thank-you is added to first or VIP orders and tied to a tracked action (a referral code, a VIP invite), then reorder or referral can be measured against a control instead of guessed.
does_not_apply_when: The insert is generic filler with no personal note and no tracked action

signal.check: First or VIP orders ship with no personal insert, or with generic filler that adds cost with no tracked purpose.

expected_effect.size: cost cents to a few dollars per insert; a vendor case reports 3.4% to 13.6% conversion on the fuller welcome-kit version, unaudited

risk.note: A packing addition; low cost per order.

prerequisites: A packing process that can add an item
A response device (code or tracked link)
steps: Pick a low-cost item: a sticker, sample or small gift, cents to a few dollars.
Pair it with a genuinely handwritten thank-you, not printed to look handwritten.
Tie it to a tracked action: a referral code, a VIP invite, or a tracked reorder offer.
Randomize by order id: half of eligible orders get the insert, half do not.
Track reorder and referral code use vs control.

test.method: Compare reorder rate and referral code use, inserted vs non-inserted orders.

title: Offer a considered-purchase feature as the gift for high-consideration categories
hypothesis: If a jewelry or other considered-purchase brand offers free engraving, a certification or appraisal guarantee, or a gifting-occasion tie-in as its wild bet gift, then the gesture fits how customers already think about the purchase instead of feeling like an unrelated freebie.

signal.check: A high-consideration or luxury category is running generic gift plays that do not connect to how the product is actually chosen or given.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: An offer addition; test on a subset of orders first.

prerequisites: Operational capacity to deliver engraving, certification or appraisal
steps: Identify the considered-purchase features customers already value (engraving, certification, appraisal, gifting tie-ins).
Pick one to offer as the wild bet gesture instead of a generic artifact.
Test on a subset of orders with a control.
Track conversion and repeat rate for the tested feature.

test.method: A/B test the feature against the standard offer.

title: Give frontline staff a standing no-approval spending budget sized to margin and AOV
hypothesis: If support and warehouse staff get a standing per-incident budget with no approval needed, sized to this brand's margin and AOV rather than a luxury hotel's figure, then reps can act on a real cue in the moment instead of losing the chance while waiting for sign-off.

signal.check: Reps notice a moment worth a small gesture (a trip mentioned, a milestone) but have no budget or authority to act without approval.

expected_effect.size: example budget $50 to $200 per incident, scaled from a luxury hotel's $2,000 against about $250,000 guest LTV (about 0.8% of LTV per incident, derived); no ecommerce lift figure

risk.note: An unguarded budget can be abused without the caps in the next idea; pair the two.

prerequisites: Customer LTV, AOV and gross margin figures to size the budget
steps: Calculate this brand's own LTV, AOV and gross margin.
Size a per-incident budget as a small share of LTV, not a copied luxury-hotel figure.
Write the rule: neutral or positive state gets a surprise on a real cue; a failure gets the fix first.
Train reps to catch cues and log every spend against the order id.

test.method: Compare repeat rate and NPS of touched customers vs a matched untouched group.
test.read_point: 90 days after the budget goes live

title: Train reps to tie frontline spend to a specific cue the customer mentioned
hypothesis: If reps spend the frontline budget on a specific item tied to something the customer actually said (a trip, a hobby, a life event), then the gesture feels personal instead of like a generic discount handed out at random.

signal.check: Frontline spend is happening with no link to anything the customer actually said in the ticket, chat or call.

expected_effect.size: unknown; case examples (a hiking trip, a vacation) are illustrations, no rate given

risk.note: A training and process step for an existing budget.

prerequisites: The frontline no-approval budget already in place
steps: Train reps to listen for cues in tickets, chats and calls (a trip, a hobby, a life event).
Require every spend to name the specific cue it responds to.
Pick an item tied to the cue (a trail map for a hiking trip, a local treat for a vacation).
Log the cue alongside the spend for later review.

test.method: Audit a sample of frontline spends for a documented, relevant cue.

title: Set per-incident, per-rep and per-customer caps on frontline spend, logged to the order id
