hypothesis: If frontline spend is capped per incident, per rep per month, and per customer, and logged against the order id, then the program cannot be quietly abused or drift into an unbounded cost line.

signal.check: A frontline discretionary budget exists with no per-incident, per-rep, or per-customer cap, or with no logging.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source calls its own guidance thin on logging, limits and review; this fills that gap

risk.note: A control step for an existing budget.

prerequisites: The frontline no-approval budget already in place
steps: Set a per-incident cap, a per-rep monthly cap, and a per-customer cap over a set period.
Require every spend to log customer, cue, item, cost and the order id.
Review the spend log weekly for any cap breaches or abuse patterns.
Adjust caps only after a review, not ad hoc.

test.method: Weekly review of the spend log against the caps.

title: Only use the frontline budget on customers in a neutral or positive state
hypothesis: If the frontline discretionary budget is reserved for customers in a neutral or positive state and a failure always gets fixed first, then the budget builds goodwill instead of substituting for a fix the customer actually needed.

signal.check: A rep is considering a gift or gesture for a customer who still has an unresolved failure (late, broken, billing).

expected_effect.size: a service study found delight in a failure state adds only negligible loyalty gain; no ecommerce figure

risk.note: A gating rule for an existing budget.

prerequisites: The exclusion list of customers with an open or recent failure
steps: Check the customer's state against the exclusion list before any frontline spend.
If in a failure state, fix the issue first with no gift attached to the fix.
Only after the fix is confirmed, allow a small, non-templated gesture if appropriate.
For volunteered hardship, follow the cancellation and hardship rule instead of a generic gesture.

test.method: Audit frontline spends against the exclusion list.

title: Write the frontline gesture into a standing support macro
hypothesis: If a frontline gesture that worked becomes a standing rule in support macros, then every eligible order gets the same treatment instead of depending on which rep happened to notice.

signal.check: A frontline gesture worked as a one-off but has not been written into a support macro or standing rule.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a standardization step, no case figure

risk.note: A documentation update to the support process.

prerequisites: A gesture that has passed at least one control read
steps: Identify a frontline gesture that showed a repeat or NPS lift in its readout.
Write it into a support macro with the eligibility rule and cap.
Train the team on the macro so it fires consistently.
Review adherence periodically.

test.method: Audit whether eligible orders consistently receive the gesture.

title: Give reps authority to resolve without escalating and track how often they need to
hypothesis: If reps have the authority to resolve a ticket without escalating, and the store tracks how often they still have to, then support gets faster for customers and the store sees exactly where the authority gap still is.

signal.check: A high share of tickets get escalated for decisions a rep could reasonably make within a defined limit.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named as a goal in the source with no method given

risk.note: A support-process change; low risk if guardrails from the caps idea are in place.

prerequisites: Support caps and macros already defined
steps: List the decision types that currently require escalation.
For low-risk, capped decisions, give reps direct authority to resolve.
Track escalation rate for those decision types over time.
Review and expand authority as reps prove consistent judgment.

test.method: Track escalation rate for the newly authorized decision types.

title: Offer case-by-case returnless keep-it refunds under a price threshold, unadvertised
hypothesis: If damaged, perishable or hard-to-resell items under a set price get a returnless refund case by case and this is never advertised as a default policy, then return processing cost drops without inviting abuse.
does_not_apply_when: A luxury catalogue with few returns; an advertised money-back guarantee fits better there instead

signal.check: Return processing cost on low-value, perishable or hard-to-resell SKUs is high relative to the item's value.

expected_effect.size: context only: about 59% of surveyed retailers ran a keep-it policy in 2023, up from 26%; about 9% of returns are estimated fraudulent; no lift figure for repeat rate

risk.note: Turn the rule off any time; watch for repeat-claimer abuse.

prerequisites: Cost per return, resale recovery rate, and return reasons by SKU
steps: Set a price threshold from this brand's own return cost data (source example: under $20).
Write eligible reasons, eligible SKUs, and a per-customer claim cap.
Randomize eligible return requests: half get keep-it, half follow standard returns as a control.
Log every keep-it claim and review for fraud signals weekly.
Raise the threshold only after keep-it recipients beat the control on repeat rate and claims stay rare.

test.method: Compare repeat-purchase rate, cost per return and claims per customer, keep-it vs standard-return control.
test.read_point: 1 month of sends, reviewed at 90 days for reorder

title: Set the keep-it refund threshold from this store's own return cost and resale data
hypothesis: If the keep-it threshold is set where refund value is below return shipping plus handling plus expected resale loss, then the policy pays for itself instead of copying another store's arbitrary cutoff.

signal.check: A keep-it threshold is being copied from another source (such as under $20) with no check against this store's own return economics.

expected_effect.size: context: return processing can cost 20% to 65% of COGS, sometimes up to 100%; no formula given by any source

risk.note: A calculation step before setting the policy.

prerequisites: Cost per return (shipping plus handling)
Resale recovery rate
Return reasons by SKU
steps: Pull cost per return (shipping plus handling) and resale recovery rate by SKU.
Compute: keep-it pays when return shipping plus handling plus expected resale loss exceeds the refund cost.
Set the threshold at the price point where this holds true, before fraud risk.
Recheck the threshold whenever shipping or resale costs change materially.

test.method: Recompute the break-even threshold quarterly against updated cost data.

title: Raise the keep-it threshold only after a passed control and rare claims
hypothesis: If the keep-it refund threshold only goes up after recipients beat the control on repeat purchase and claims per customer stay rare, then the policy expands based on proof instead of assumption.

signal.check: A keep-it pilot is running and someone wants to raise the threshold before the review date or without checking claims-per-customer.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a lift figure for raising the threshold

risk.note: A gating decision on an already-running pilot.

prerequisites: A keep-it pilot already running with a control
steps: Wait for the pilot's planned review date.
Check repeat-purchase or 90-day reorder rate of keep-it recipients vs control.
Check claims per customer for any spike in repeat claimers.
Raise the threshold only if both checks pass; otherwise hold or lower it.

test.method: Compare repeat rate and claims per customer at each review point.
test.read_point: At each pilot's planned review date

title: Offer a lifetime warranty only on the most durable SKUs, repair-first
hypothesis: If a lifetime warranty or repair-for-life promise is limited to the most durable SKUs, repair-first with defined scope and exclusions, and modeled against expected claims first, then the promise removes a real buying objection without creating a claims cost that overwhelms margin.
does_not_apply_when: Thin margins that cannot absorb modeled claims cost; delay the warranty until margin improves

signal.check: Customers hesitate to buy a durable product because they doubt it will last, and no warranty exists to answer that doubt.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources warn that generous guarantees can be pulled back once claims 'bury' the brand on products that do not last

risk.note: Existing promises must be honored even if the guarantee is later closed to new orders.

prerequisites: Defect and failure rates by SKU
Legal review of warranty terms
steps: Model expected claims, repair logistics and cost for the most durable SKUs only.
Write repair-first terms with clear scope and exclusions.
Publish a clear, friendly claims page after legal review.
Track claims rate and cost per claim by SKU; delay on thin-margin SKUs.

test.method: A/B the guarantee on the covered SKU's PDP against no guarantee.
test.read_point: 60 to 90 days plus the claim window

title: Offer a specific, measurable outcome guarantee and track refund rate before scaling
hypothesis: If a physical product guarantee promises one specific, measurable outcome with a clear, product-appropriate remedy for a substantiated claim, and refund rate is tracked before scaling, then the guarantee can lift conversion without an unmanaged refund cost.
does_not_apply_when: No specific outcome can be named; a 'keep working until you get results' promise belongs to services

signal.check: A guarantee is being proposed with a vague or open-ended promise instead of one specific outcome and remedy.

expected_effect.size: a book-summary claim from a services context reports about 30% more sales with refunds barely up; not an ecommerce benchmark

risk.note: Close the guarantee to new orders if refunds rise; existing claims must still be honored.

prerequisites: A refund rate baseline before the guarantee
Legal review of the claim
steps: Pick one specific, measurable outcome the product produces.
Write a clear, product-appropriate remedy for a substantiated claim.
A/B the guarantee on the PDP against the current page.
Track refund rate before and after; scale only if refunds barely move.

test.method: A/B test conversion with vs without the guarantee, and track refund rate over time.
test.read_point: 60 to 90 days plus the claim window

title: Test risk-reversal offers only where product quality is high and returns are controlled
hypothesis: If a risk-reversal offer only runs on SKUs with high product quality and monitored return abuse, then it can convert and cut friction without becoming a magnet for fraud or expensive returns.
does_not_apply_when: Product quality is unproven or return abuse is not monitored

signal.check: A risk-reversal or money-back offer is being proposed for a SKU with unresolved quality issues or no return-abuse monitoring.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no case figure given for risk reversal alone

risk.note: Close the offer if return abuse rises.

prerequisites: Product quality data (review rating, defect rate)
Return abuse monitoring in place
steps: Check product quality signals (review rating, defect rate) before proposing risk reversal.
Confirm return abuse monitoring (repeat claimers, mismatched reasons) is active.
Run the offer only on qualifying SKUs, with a PDP A/B test.
Track return rate and abuse signals alongside conversion.

test.method: A/B test conversion with vs without risk reversal, and monitor return rate.

title: Lock in price for loyal subscribers, ring-fenced and modeled against cost trends
hypothesis: If a price lock is offered only to a defined group of loyal subscribers, marketed as a loyalty benefit, and modeled against future unit cost trends first, then it can lift retention without becoming an unfunded promise on thin margins.
does_not_apply_when: Margins are thin and unit cost trends have not been modeled

signal.check: A subscription price lock or similar loyalty promise is being considered with no model of future unit cost trends.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a historical case (a 2012 price lock) is context, not a transferable lift figure

risk.note: A price lock already granted must be honored even if costs rise faster than modeled.

prerequisites: Cost trend per unit modeled forward
steps: Ring-fence who qualifies (for example, current subscribers at the time of launch).
Model future unit cost trends before promising the lock.
Market it as a loyalty benefit, kept narrow if margins are thin.
Test on an eligible cohort and measure retention vs non-locked subscribers.

test.method: Compare retention of locked vs non-locked subscribers.

title: Put a real, safe product test in the box only if the product actually wins it
hypothesis: If a safe, readable, non-selective product test is put in the first box only when the product truly wins it against rivals, then the test builds trust and repeat purchase instead of risking a customer catching a rigged comparison.
does_not_apply_when: The product does not clearly win the test, or the test is unsafe or unreadable by a normal customer

signal.check: A proof-in-the-box idea is being considered without first running the test privately against rivals to confirm the product wins.

expected_effect.size: a cited case's revenue growth does not show the kit caused it; no lift figure isolated for the test alone

risk.note: A failed or unsafe test in the box can damage trust; validate privately first.

prerequisites: A private test run against rivals confirming a win
steps: Pick one attribute the product can prove and that wins against rivals.
Run the test privately against rivals first to confirm it is safe, readable and not selective.
Put the test in the first box for half of first orders as a randomized test.
Measure conversion to second order vs the control group with no test.

test.method: Randomize half of first orders to receive the test; compare second-order rate.

title: Track damaged-in-transit reports as a cheaper fix than a keep-it policy
hypothesis: If damaged-in-transit reports and packaging quality are tracked as a return-cost driver alongside the keep-it break-even, then a packaging fix can lower cost per return more cheaply than a keep-it policy or a warranty.

signal.check: Return cost is being addressed only through keep-it or warranty policy, with no check on whether damage in transit is a bigger driver.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: A diagnostic and packaging-improvement step.

prerequisites: Return reason data broken out by SKU, including damage-in-transit
steps: Pull return reasons by SKU and isolate the damaged-in-transit share.
Compare the cost of a packaging fix to the cost of a keep-it or warranty policy for those SKUs.
Fix packaging first where it is the cheaper lever.
Re-measure damaged-in-transit rate after the fix.

test.method: Compare damaged-in-transit rate and cost per return before and after the packaging fix.

title: Offer a landed-cost or customs-duty guarantee for cross-border and diaspora buyers
hypothesis: If cross-border or diaspora buyers see landed cost shown at checkout, or a promise to cover surprise duties, then a known objection for international buyers gets removed before it costs the sale.

signal.check: A meaningful share of orders come from cross-border or diaspora buyers and checkout shows no landed-cost transparency or duty guarantee.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: A duty guarantee creates a real cost exposure if duties are higher than modeled; cap and fund it.

prerequisites: Landed-cost calculation capability at checkout
Order volume forecast by destination country
steps: Identify the top cross-border or diaspora destinations by order volume.
Add landed-cost display at checkout for those destinations, or model a duty-coverage guarantee.
Fund the maximum modeled duty exposure before promising coverage.
Track checkout conversion for those destinations before and after.

test.method: Compare checkout-to-order conversion for the affected destinations before and after the change.

title: Run an advertised money-back guarantee as its own tracked test, separate from the unadvertised keep-it pilot
hypothesis: If the owner wants a publicly advertised no-return money-back guarantee, it runs as its own bounded test with refund-rate tracking and a PDP A/B split, kept separate from the unadvertised case-by-case keep-it pilot, so the two do not get confused or run on the same cohort.

signal.check: The team is tempted to advertise the keep-it pilot publicly as a marketing guarantee, mixing an unadvertised pilot with a public promise.

expected_effect.size: one case credits an advertised 30-day no-return guarantee for scaling; no method given, and it conflicts with the sources' fraud caution

risk.note: An advertised guarantee is a public promise; close it to new orders if refunds rise.

prerequisites: A keep-it pilot already running
Refund rate baseline
steps: Decide whether the owner wants an advertised guarantee or the quieter keep-it pilot; do not run both on the same cohort.
If advertised, treat it as a new outcome-guarantee bet (P15) with its own PDP A/B test.
Track refund rate before and after separately from the keep-it pilot's numbers.
Never raise the keep-it threshold using the advertised guarantee's results, or vice versa.

test.method: A/B test the advertised guarantee on the PDP; track refund rate against the pre-guarantee baseline.

title: Let subscribers pause easily and roll over credit instead of just cancelling
hypothesis: If subscribers get an easy pause option with credit rollover and cadence control, then more of them pause instead of cancelling outright when their circumstances change temporarily.

signal.check: The subscription tool has no easy pause option, or pausing forfeits already-paid credit.

expected_effect.size: case claims 'massive retention gains' and 90% subscriber retention with custom cadence; no method given for either

risk.note: A subscription-tool configuration change.

prerequisites: Subscription tool supports pause, skip and credit rollover
steps: Confirm the subscription tool supports pause, skip and cadence changes.
Turn on easy self-serve pause with credit rollover, not just cancel.
Allow subscribers to adjust cadence without contacting support.
Track pause vs cancel rate after the change.

test.method: Compare pause-to-resume rate and overall churn before and after enabling easy pause.

title: Proactively flag overstocked subscribers and suggest a pause to save money
hypothesis: If subscribers receiving product faster than they use it get a proactive email suggesting a pause, framed as protecting their wallet, then they resume later instead of cancelling out of frustration at wasted product.

signal.check: No process flags subscribers whose shipments are outpacing their actual consumption.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source names the mechanic and gives no threshold or lift figure

risk.note: A proactive email; the subscriber decides whether to pause.

prerequisites: Consumption rate per SKU, order cadence, skip and pause history
steps: Compare shipments received with consumption per SKU to flag overstocked subscribers.
Set a threshold for overstocked from this brand's own data.
Email flagged subscribers suggesting a pause to save money, not framed as a retention tactic.
Track resume vs cancel after pause, vs a flagged-but-not-emailed control group.

test.method: Compare resume and cancel rate, emailed vs flagged-not-emailed control.

title: Never delay a subscription cancellation; offer a gentle, non-blocking pause option instead
hypothesis: If cancellation always completes on request, with only an optional reason field and a one-line pause offer that does not block the cancel, then customers trust the brand more even at the moment they are leaving, and some come back later.
does_not_apply_when: Volunteered hardship: an approved remedy like pause or a refund can be offered, still without delay

signal.check: The current cancel flow uses a save-offer wall, forced calls, or multiple steps before cancellation completes.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source measures this directly, it is a stated policy correction to a common practice

risk.note: A flow simplification; removes friction rather than adding it.

prerequisites: Subscription tool cancel flow that can be edited
steps: Remove any save-offer wall or forced multi-step process from the cancel flow.
Add an optional reason field and a one-line pause offer that does not block cancellation.
Complete the cancellation immediately on request regardless of the reason given.
For volunteered hardship, offer an approved remedy without delaying the request.

test.method: Track time-to-cancel and resume rate after the pause offer, before and after the flow change.

title: Add a small unbranded surprise inside subscription boxes as the wild bet
hypothesis: If subscription boxes carry an occasional unbranded artifact, surprise upgrade or discretionary treat, with cadence control and pause and rollover already in place, then the subscription itself becomes the wild bet's delivery vehicle without extra shipping cost.

signal.check: Subscription boxes ship the same contents every cycle with no surprise element and no plan to add one.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this is a card writer's synthesis, no case figure

risk.note: Check COGS impact of the added item before scaling.

prerequisites: Cadence control, pause and rollover already working
Margin per bundle checked
steps: Check the COGS impact of adding a small item to a subset of boxes.
Pick a random cadence for the surprise, not tied to a fixed cycle.
Ship to a randomized subset with a control group receiving the standard box.
Track churn and referral for both groups.

test.method: Compare subscription churn and referral, surprise vs standard box.

title: Treat the first 100 days after signup as the main churn window
hypothesis: If the first 100 days after a first purchase gets a planned emotional journey instead of an immediate cross-sell or review request, then early churn drops because the customer feels cared for during the highest-risk window.

signal.check: New customers get a cross-sell email or review request within days of their first order, with no planned journey for the first 100 days.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source names an 8-phase model without listing the phases, and gives no lift figure

risk.note: A lifecycle sequence change; test on a subset first.

prerequisites: Repurchase interval and early churn baseline
steps: Remove cross-sell and review-ask messaging from the first 100 days.
Plan an emotional journey: a welcome kit, sequential founder videos, or surprise digital upgrades.
Randomize new customers into the journey or the standard flow.
Measure repurchase rate and early churn at 100 days.

test.method: Compare repurchase rate and early churn, journey vs standard flow.

title: Add a proactive delivery check-in around the expected arrival date
hypothesis: If a proactive message checks whether the order arrived and fits, timed to the expected delivery date and separate from the 100-day churn window, then problems surface early instead of turning into a silent return or a bad review.

signal.check: No message checks in with the customer around the expected delivery date; the first contact after shipping is often a review request weeks later.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: A lifecycle email or message addition.

prerequisites: Expected delivery date data per order
steps: Trigger a check-in message near the expected delivery date asking if the order arrived and fits.
Route any negative response straight to support, not a survey queue.
Keep this separate from the 100-day onboarding journey.
Track resulting return or complaint rate against a group with no check-in.

test.method: Compare return and complaint rate for orders with vs without the check-in.

title: Add expiring loyalty value with disclosed terms and a meaningful earn rate
hypothesis: If loyalty points or coins expire on a disclosed schedule with a meaningful earn rate and multi-channel reminders worded as 'you earned this, don't waste it', then expiry becomes a reason to return instead of a source of complaints.
does_not_apply_when: A low earn rate or impractical redemption; expiry then feels punitive, not motivating

signal.check: A loyalty program exists in a repeat category with no expiry mechanic, or an existing expiry with undisclosed terms or a low earn rate.

expected_effect.size: one case reports 12.4% of signups came through the loyalty system and a '70X ROI' on tooling, both undefined; a 60-day expiry example

risk.note: A poorly run expiry can generate complaints; run the fairness checklist first.

prerequisites: A loyalty app with expiry and reminder triggers
SMS and email consent
steps: Disclose the expiry window and terms before customers earn any value.
Confirm the earn rate is meaningful and redemption is practical before adding expiry.
Set reminders on 2 or more channels with consent, worded as loss of earned value.
Track redemption, repeat rate vs a no-expiry control cohort, and complaints per 1,000 reminders.

test.method: Compare repeat rate and complaint rate, expiry vs no-expiry control cohort.
test.read_point: 2 expiry cycles (about 120 days at a 60-day expiry)

title: Track what share of new signups come through the loyalty program
hypothesis: If the store measures the share of new signups that come through the loyalty program, then it can decide whether loyalty is a real acquisition surface worth investing in or a commodity feature not worth a wild bet.

signal.check: No one tracks what share of new customer signups originate from the loyalty program versus other channels.

expected_effect.size: one case reports 12.4% of signups via loyalty; not a target, a single example

risk.note: A measurement step against existing signup data.

prerequisites: Signup source tracking
steps: Pull new signup counts by source, including loyalty program signups.
Compute the loyalty share of total new signups over a recent period.
If the share is material, treat loyalty as a surface for expiring value or status rewards.
If not, do not build a wild bet on the loyalty program as an acquisition channel.

test.method: Recompute the loyalty signup share whenever a loyalty-related bet is considered.
test.read_point: Before any loyalty-based wild bet, then quarterly

title: Run a seasonal daily-reveal calendar with one genuinely valuable offer a day
hypothesis: If a seasonal calendar reveals one genuinely valuable offer per day with a midnight expiry and clear rules up front, and no filler days, then customers keep coming back daily instead of losing interest after a weak day breaks the loop.
does_not_apply_when: Run year-round; repeating daily urgency all year trains discount dependency instead of feeling special

signal.check: A seasonal promotional calendar is planned with filler days or offers that are not genuinely valuable.

expected_effect.size: one case's headline '82% Return Rate' is undefined in the source; not usable as a benchmark

risk.note: A seasonal, time-boxed program.

prerequisites: 12 distinct, genuinely valuable offers planned in advance
steps: Plan a genuinely valuable offer for each of the 12 days in advance; cut any filler day.
Set a calendar gate with midnight expiry and a visible 'missed' state.
Announce the rules up front so customers know what to expect.
Run this only as a seasonal window, not a year-round mechanic.

test.method: Track daily visit and conversion rate across the calendar window.
test.read_point: Daily during the window, summarized at the end

title: Delay the discount to the next purchase instead of the current order
hypothesis: If a reward unlocks on the next purchase instead of the current one, with a clear expiry and a message about the value earned, then the customer has a reason to come back instead of the discount just shrinking today's margin.
does_not_apply_when: A one-time-purchase category, where a delayed reward has nothing to attach to

signal.check: Discounts are only ever applied to the current order, with no mechanic that rewards a future purchase.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no case figure given, this is a mechanic description

risk.note: Creates an accounting liability for unredeemed rewards; track it.

prerequisites: A way to unlock and message a future-order reward
steps: Set no discount on the current order; the reward unlocks after purchase for the next one.
Set an expiry window that is neither too long (kills urgency) nor too short (feels punishing).
Message the earned value clearly ('you have $X waiting').
Test the unlock threshold and expiry window against a no-reward control; record the liability.

test.method: A/B test the delayed-discount cohort against a no-reward control.

title: Make a paid loyalty tier about exclusive access, not just discount
hypothesis: If a paid loyalty tier centers on exclusive access (early drops, events, a founder channel) rather than only a discount, then members feel they are buying status, and the tier can be judged on spend and retention lift vs comparable non-members.

signal.check: A paid loyalty tier is being designed around a bigger discount rather than exclusive access or status benefits.

expected_effect.size: a reported figure (via a blog, no method given): paid members up to 60% more likely to increase spend, twice the free-program rate

risk.note: A tier design decision; test before a full rollout.

prerequisites: A membership or loyalty platform that supports paid tiers
steps: Design the paid tier's core benefit as access (early drops, events, direct founder contact), not a bigger discount.
Set the price to reflect access value, not just a discount subsidy.
Build a matched comparison group of non-members for measurement.
Track spend and retention lift vs the matched group, not signup count.

test.method: Compare spend and retention, paid members vs matched non-members.

title: Reward non-purchase actions with gifts and invites, and let engagement move members between tiers
hypothesis: If reviews, UGC and other non-purchase actions earn gifts and event invites, and engagement can move a member up within tiers, then loyalty stops being only about how much someone spent and starts rewarding advocacy too.

signal.check: The loyalty or VIP program rewards only purchase amount, with no recognition for reviews, UGC or referrals.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source names the mechanic (The Body Shop's tiered program), no lift figure given

risk.note: A program design addition.

prerequisites: A loyalty or VIP tiering system that can track non-purchase actions
steps: Define which non-purchase actions count (reviews, UGC, referrals).
Set gifts or invites as the reward for those actions.
Allow engagement points to move a member up within tiers, alongside spend.
Track review count and UGC volume before and after the change.

test.method: Compare review count and UGC volume before and after the engagement-reward mechanic launches.

title: Run mystery bundles or blind boxes only with a stated minimum value and profitable products
hypothesis: If a mystery bundle states a minimum guaranteed value and only includes products already profitable at the bundle discount, then it can move slow or excess stock at a real margin instead of training buyers to expect a loss-making deal.

signal.check: A mystery bundle or blind box idea is on the table with no stated minimum value or with products not yet confirmed profitable at the discount.

expected_effect.size: example: 6 bundles, 5 to 8 items, up to 50% off, run in early November; no repeat-purchase or margin lift figure given

risk.note: Check gambling-style-mechanics rules before running blind boxes in some markets.

prerequisites: Products confirmed profitable at the bundle discount
Gambling-style mechanics rules checked for the market
steps: State a minimum guaranteed value for the bundle ('at least $X value guaranteed').
Include only products already profitable at the bundle discount.
Run it first on a small loyalty segment, not the full list.
Measure margin at the bundle price and full-price repeat purchase after; slow the cadence if buyers start waiting for bundles.

test.method: Track margin per bundle sold and full-price repeat purchase rate afterward.
test.read_point: After the bundle run, then again at the next planned run

title: Build a named, invite-only VIP tier for the top 1% by lifetime spend
hypothesis: If the top 1% of customers by lifetime spend get a named, invite-only tier with early drop access, a founder channel, and a surprise insert in every order, then their retention and AOV can be tested against non-VIP customers before formalizing a second tier.

signal.check: No named VIP tier exists for the top spenders, and revenue share of the top 1% has never been measured.

expected_effect.size: reported cases (a status app with 13 million+ monthly actives; a motorcycle club whose members spend 30% more on clothing and events) are not ecommerce tier-lift figures

risk.note: Existing members keep their tier if invites stop; low ongoing risk.

prerequisites: Revenue share of top 1% measured
A loyalty or membership tool
steps: Measure the actual revenue share of the top 1% before building the tier.
Rank by lifetime spend and invite the top 1%.
Give benefits worth the friction: early drop access, a direct founder channel, a surprise insert in every order.
Compare VIP retention and AOV to a matched non-VIP group at 90 days; add a second tier only on a pass.

test.method: Compare retention and AOV, VIP vs matched non-VIP (for example, the next 2% to 3% of spenders).

title: Only gate a benefit behind friction when the reward is worth it
hypothesis: If access is gated behind a waitlist, invite or referral only when the reward inside is worth the friction, and benefits stay clearly tied to loyalty, then the gate builds desire instead of just shrinking the funnel for no reason.

signal.check: A gate (waitlist, invite-only, referral requirement) is being added without checking whether the reward behind it is strong enough to justify the friction.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source's ecommerce case (a gated men's grooming brand) is an example, not a rate

risk.note: A design check before launching a gate.

prerequisites: A defined reward behind the gate
steps: Name the reward behind the gate and check it is strong enough to want, not just access for its own sake.
Keep benefits clearly tied to loyalty status so a leak does not look arbitrary or unfair.
Test signup interest before vs after adding the gate, if possible.
Remove or redesign the gate if desire before it is low.

test.method: Compare signup or interest rate with and without the gate, where feasible.

title: Run limited drops with real, fixed scarcity, no fake countdowns
hypothesis: If a limited drop uses fixed inventory, a fixed release time and numbered batches, with no fake countdown timers or unkept restock promises, then scarcity feels real, which the sources link to selling out at full price.
does_not_apply_when: No audience has been built yet; a drop with no pre-built audience may sell nothing

signal.check: A drop or launch uses a countdown timer or urgency messaging with no real inventory or time constraint behind it.

expected_effect.size: case examples describe selling out in seconds to minutes at full price; no rate given for a typical store

risk.note: Unsold stock at the end of a drop returns to normal sale; low financial risk if inventory is sized carefully.

prerequisites: An audience already built
A hero product developed and tested
An SMS or email list with consent
steps: Fix inventory, release time and cadence (for example, weekly, or a set day each cycle).
Tell insiders (VIP tier or consented SMS list) the day before.
Gate access with a waiting room or single-use links so members, not bots, get in.
Price at full price; design the packaging and unboxing reveal as part of the product.
Log sell-through time, buyer overlap across drops, and any reseller listings.

test.method: Track full-price sell-through and reseller capture over 3 drops.
test.read_point: After each drop, reviewed across 3 drops

title: Build the brand and audience before running the first limited drop
hypothesis: If the brand spends real time building an audience and testing the product before the first drop, then the first drop has a real chance to sell out instead of launching to no one.

signal.check: A drop is being planned before the brand has any meaningful audience (email list, SMS list, or social following) built up.

expected_effect.size: case examples: about 1 year of brand building and 20 tested box designs before the first sale; 6 months of audience building before a first shoe launch

risk.note: A sequencing decision before spending on a drop launch.

prerequisites: None beyond time and consistent content or outreach
steps: Set a minimum audience size (email or SMS list, or engaged following) before scheduling the first drop.
Spend the lead time testing the product and building anticipation, not just marketing a date.
Delay the first drop date if the audience has not reached the minimum.
Track list growth weekly leading up to the planned drop.

test.method: Compare list size at drop time against the minimum set in planning.
test.read_point: Before the first drop is scheduled

title: Gate drop access with a waiting room or single-use links, and tell insiders first
hypothesis: If drop access is gated through an invite-only waiting room, single-use links or a queue fast-pass, and insiders are told the day before, then members get in ahead of bots and resellers instead of losing the drop to automated buying.

signal.check: A past drop sold out to resellers or bots faster than real fans could access it, with no gating in place.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no rate given, this is a gating mechanic

risk.note: A technical gating setup for the drop.

prerequisites: A waiting room or single-use-link tool
An SMS or VIP list with consent
steps: Set up an invite-only waiting room, single-use links, or a queue fast-pass for the drop.
Tell insiders (VIP tier or consented SMS list) about the drop the day before.
Monitor for bot or reseller patterns during the drop window.
Review buyer overlap and any reseller listings after the drop.

test.method: Compare reseller listings and buyer overlap before and after gating is added.

title: Raise the drop batch size if real fans get shut out at full price
hypothesis: If batch size increases whenever real fans complain about being shut out and the product still sells out at full price, then the brand captures more revenue without flooding the market or killing scarcity.

signal.check: Drops consistently sell out in seconds with visible fan complaints about missing out, at the same batch size every time.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no rate given, this is a supply-sizing rule

risk.note: Increasing batch size gradually and re-checking sell-through each time.

prerequisites: Sell-through time and fan complaint data from prior drops
steps: Track sell-through time and fan complaints after each drop.
If fans are consistently shut out and it still sells at full price, raise the batch size for the next drop.
Re-check sell-through time at the new batch size.
Stop raising batch size once sell-through slows below full price.

test.method: Compare sell-through time and price realized across successive batch sizes.

title: Keep a drop cadence only while it tracks repeat visits or purchase frequency
hypothesis: If drop cadence continues only while it still tracks with repeat visits or purchase frequency, and the supply chain can support it, then the store avoids running drops so often that they stop feeling special or straining operations.
does_not_apply_when: The supply chain cannot support a fast cadence yet

signal.check: Drop frequency has been increased without checking whether repeat visits or purchase frequency are still rising alongside it.

expected_effect.size: one case reports 15 to 20 days design-to-shelf and 200 to 250 styles a month as a fast-cadence example; not a target

risk.note: A fast cadence without supply-chain readiness can strain operations and unsold stock.

prerequisites: Visit and purchase frequency data by drop week
steps: Track visit and purchase frequency around each drop.
Confirm the supply chain can support the current or a faster cadence before increasing it.
If frequency stops tracking with cadence, slow down and run fewer, better drops instead.
Review this quarterly as the drop program matures.

test.method: Compare visit and purchase frequency trend against drop cadence changes.

title: Design the packaging and unboxing reveal as part of the drop product
hypothesis: If the packaging and the unboxing moment are designed as part of the drop, not an afterthought, then the reveal itself becomes part of what customers pay for and share.

signal.check: A drop's packaging is standard shipping material with no design thought given to the unboxing moment.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources name this as part of the model without a lift figure

risk.note: A design and cost decision for the packaging line.

prerequisites: Budget allocated for premium packaging
steps: Design the outer box, inner presentation and reveal sequence intentionally.
Test the unboxing with a few real customers before the drop, watching for share-worthy moments.
Factor packaging cost into the drop's cash cap.
Track UGC (photos, unboxing posts) from the drop's buyers.

test.method: Track UGC volume from the drop's buyers vs a standard-packaging baseline.

title: Sell access and status, not just price, on the top tier or a drop
hypothesis: If the top tier or a drop is positioned around the feeling of having what others don't, not around price, then customers buy into status and identity, which is harder for a competitor to copy with a cheaper price.

signal.check: Marketing for a top tier or drop leads with price or discount messaging instead of access and status.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source's comparison (a hard-to-book restaurant reservation) is an analogy, not a rate

risk.note: A positioning and messaging decision.

prerequisites: An existing top tier or drop program
steps: Audit current messaging for the top tier or drop for price-led language.
Rewrite it around access, scarcity and identity instead of savings.
Test the new messaging on the next drop or tier communication.
Track AOV and repeat purchase among the targeted segment.

test.method: Compare AOV and repeat purchase before and after the messaging shift.

title: Run a livestream selling event with compressed buy windows for demonstrable products
hypothesis: If a livestream event with checkout in the stream runs for products that reward demonstration or storytelling, then full-price sell-through in the stream can be compared directly to the same SKU sold normally on site.

signal.check: The product benefits from being shown in use, but the store has never tried a compressed-window live-selling event.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no ecommerce-specific case figure given

risk.note: A one-off event; low ongoing risk if platform features are confirmed first.

prerequisites: Live shopping features on the chosen platform confirmed for the country
steps: Confirm live shopping and in-stream checkout features are available on the chosen platform in the brand's country.
Pick a demonstrable or collectible product and plan a timed listing or event.
Run the event with checkout available in the stream.
Compare full-price sell-through in the stream vs the same SKU sold normally on site.

test.method: Compare sell-through and price realized, live event vs normal site sale.
test.read_point: Immediately after the event, and 7 days after for any residual orders

title: Show a genuine per-SKU low-stock indicator for stores that never run scheduled drops
hypothesis: If a catalogue store that never runs drops shows a real, accurate low-stock count per SKU, then it gets an honest scarcity signal without adopting the drop model it does not use.
does_not_apply_when: The store already runs scheduled drops; use real drop scarcity instead of a low-stock flag

signal.check: A catalogue store with genuinely limited stock on some SKUs shows no low-stock indicator anywhere on the PDP.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: Must reflect real inventory; a fake count would break trust.

prerequisites: Real-time or near-real-time inventory count per SKU
steps: Confirm inventory data is accurate and current enough to show live.
Add a real remaining-count or low-stock flag to PDPs where stock is genuinely limited.
Never show it on SKUs with ample stock.
Track PDP-to-cart conversion for flagged SKUs before and after.

test.method: Compare PDP-to-cart conversion for flagged SKUs before and after the indicator appears.

title: Run a tiered referral waitlist that gates a launch behind escalating product rewards
hypothesis: If a launch is gated behind a waitlist with unique referral links and escalating product rewards, never cash, then referral signups can be tracked against a 30% share pass mark instead of guessed at.

signal.check: A launch or drop is planned with a plain email signup form, no referral mechanic and no fraud filter plan.

expected_effect.size: case example: 100,000+ emails in 1 week, about 85% legitimate, 77% from referrals; pass mark heuristic is referral signups above 30% of total

risk.note: Fraud can inflate signups; verify emails and cap rewards per device before honoring them.

prerequisites: A launch or drop to gate
A waitlist tool with referral links
A fraud filter plan
steps: Gate the launch behind a waitlist; give each signup a unique referral link.
Set escalating, reachable product or access rewards, never cash.
Show a live progress bar toward the next reward.
Plan fraud filtering: verify emails, cap rewards per IP or device, hold rewards until launch.
Track referral share of signups; pass mark is referral signups above 30% of total.

test.method: Compare referral share of signups and legitimate share against the 30% pass mark.
test.read_point: At the midpoint and close of the pre-launch window

title: Build a named community with real rituals and ongoing programming
hypothesis: If a named community gets real rituals, status markers and ongoing programming (a sticker and note in every box, UGC contests, consistent voice), then it becomes a real hub instead of a hashtag that fades.

signal.check: The brand calls its customers a 'community' with no named identity, ritual or ongoing programming behind it.

expected_effect.size: reported cases: a named community grew from 800,000 to over 3 million members in 2 years; a motorcycle club's members spend 30% more on clothing and events

risk.note: A branding and programming investment; low direct risk.

prerequisites: A consistent brand voice
A capacity to run ongoing programming (contests, events)
steps: Name the community and give it a real identity, not just a hashtag.
Add a small ritual (a sticker and welcome note in every box).
Run UGC contests with consistent voice and visible follow-through.
Treat social as a hub for two-way conversation, not a broadcast channel.

test.method: Track UGC volume and community size growth over time.

title: Run a co-creation program where the community votes on new products
hypothesis: If the community can submit and vote on new product ideas, with credit and a cut for winners and a public statement of what can and cannot ship, then customers feel real ownership, and product decisions get real signal instead of guesswork.

signal.check: New product decisions are made with no input mechanism from loyal customers or VIP members.

expected_effect.size: one case requires 10,000 supporters to be considered, with about a 1% royalty of net sales to the creator; no ecommerce-scale figure

risk.note: Results can skew toward a vocal minority; weigh votes against broader sales data before committing production.

prerequisites: An existing community or VIP tier to seed the submit-and-vote page
steps: Build a submit-and-vote page seeded with the existing community or VIP tier.
Set credit and a cut of sales for winning submissions.
Publish a clear, public statement of what can and cannot actually ship.
Act visibly on the winning idea and feed the result into real product decisions.

test.method: Track votes cast, launch sell-through to voters, and repeat rate of insiders vs non-insiders.
test.read_point: At launch of the co-created product

title: Spend months building an audience before the next product launch
hypothesis: If real time (months, not weeks) goes into building an audience and gathering feedback before a new product launches, then the launch has a warm audience ready instead of starting cold.

signal.check: A new product is being planned to launch to cold traffic with no audience-building period beforehand.

expected_effect.size: one case spent about 6 months building an audience before its first product launch

risk.note: A timeline decision; delays launch but reduces launch-day risk.

prerequisites: Content or outreach capacity to sustain months of audience building
steps: Set a minimum audience-building period before the launch date (months, not weeks).
Publish content and gather feedback from the target audience during this period.
Track list and engagement growth against a target before locking the launch date.
Delay launch if the audience has not reached the target.

test.method: Compare list size and engagement at launch against the pre-set target.

title: Start an insider program tiny: hand-pick the first 10 to 20 customers
hypothesis: If the first insider program starts with 10 to 20 hand-picked customers personally reached out to, then the founder learns what works before automating or scaling any of it.

signal.check: An insider or VIP program is being designed at scale from day one, with no small hand-picked pilot first.

expected_effect.size: one case launched 20 one-of-a-kind items and personally messaged everyone who engaged; no lift figure given

risk.note: A small, manual pilot; low cost and risk.

prerequisites: Founder or team time to personally reach out
steps: Hand-pick the first 10 to 20 customers or engaged followers to invite.
Personally reach out (a DM, a call, a personal note) rather than an automated invite.
Ask for feedback and give early access as the core benefit.
Scale rituals (monthly calls, larger events) only as engagement proves out, and automate only after the pattern repeats.

test.method: Track engagement (replies, feedback given, repeat purchase) of the pilot group.

title: Publish content that gives value with no sales ask, including linking off the store's own site
hypothesis: If content consistently gives value with no sales ask, even linking to other useful things off the brand's own site, then engaged customers build real trust and a measurably higher LTV once self-selection is controlled for.

signal.check: All brand content pushes back to a product page or a sale, with nothing that would be useful even if the brand never sold anything.

expected_effect.size: a reported 3.5x LTV gap for content-engaged customers is confounded by self-selection; control for prior spend before crediting it

risk.note: A content strategy shift; low direct risk.

prerequisites: Customer-level engagement data joined to order history
steps: Ask: what content would customers consume even if the brand never sold them anything?
Publish that content consistently, including links off the brand's own site where genuinely useful.
Track engagement depth per customer.
Measure engaged-customer LTV against non-engaged, controlling for prior spend.

test.method: Compare engaged vs non-engaged LTV, controlling for prior spend.

title: Give creators freedom and seeded product instead of a tight script
hypothesis: If creators get product seeded to them and freedom to react unscripted, following disclosure rules, then their content reads as authentic and creator-attributed revenue can be tracked against product cost.

signal.check: Creator partnerships currently use a tight, over-scripted brief with no room for the creator's own reaction.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the cited cases give no numbers

risk.note: Unscripted content risks an off-brand reaction; disclosure rules must still be followed.

prerequisites: Creator disclosure rules for the platform confirmed
steps: Seed the product to selected creators with minimal scripting.
Confirm disclosure rules for the platform and region before the content goes live.
Track creator-attributed revenue using unique links or codes.
Compare revenue per creator against the seeded product's cost.

test.method: Compare creator-attributed revenue against seeding cost per creator.
test.read_point: 30 to 60 days after content goes live

title: Run a stunt whose format actually matches the brand's voice
hypothesis: If a stunt's format matches the brand voice (watchable content, a benefit-dramatizing stunt, or an anti-promotional gesture on a retail holiday), then it reads as the brand's own move instead of a borrowed format that confuses the audience.

signal.check: A stunt idea has been picked before checking whether its format (content, dramatization, anti-promotion) actually fits this brand's specific voice.

expected_effect.size: case examples: a viral drinks brand's format, a sleep-brand internship stunt, and an anti-promotional holiday gesture; no comparable rate for a small store

risk.note: A public stunt cannot be withdrawn once launched.

prerequisites: Stages 1 to 3 of the wild bets rollout passed
A confirmed brand voice
steps: Pick the format that fits this brand's specific voice: watchable content, a benefit-dramatizing stunt, or an anti-promotional gesture.
Consider a scaled-down option: paying a few customers to test and document the product publicly.
Get the owner's written confirmation the format fits before building anything.
Proceed to the legal and brand-risk review before launch.

test.method: Track coverage, shares, site traffic and sales in the window vs a matched prior window.

title: Design an anti-marketing stunt as an inside joke for the audience, not for broad reach
hypothesis: If an anti-marketing stunt is designed as a filter and an inside joke for a specific audience rather than for the widest possible reach, then it fits a commoditized category or a younger audience without needing to outspend big retailers.
does_not_apply_when: The brand cannot handle a viral spike operationally, or the audience is not a Millennial or Gen Z, filter-savvy one

signal.check: A stunt is being designed to maximize reach rather than to feel like an inside joke that filters for the brand's real audience.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no lift figure, this is a design principle for a commoditized category or younger audience

risk.note: A public stunt cannot be withdrawn; confirm site and ops can take a spike first.

prerequisites: Confirmed site and operations capacity for a traffic spike
steps: Design the stunt as a filter: something the target audience gets and outsiders might not.
Confirm site and operations can handle a sudden traffic spike.
Skip broad-reach media buys; let the joke travel through the audience itself.
Track site traffic, sales and any operational strain during the spike.

test.method: Track site traffic, checkout conversion and complaints during and after the spike.
test.read_point: During the spike and 1 week after

title: Budget a stunt against the marketing line and value it against incremental orders, not traffic alone
hypothesis: If a stunt is budgeted as a marketing cost and its earned media value is compared to incremental orders and contribution margin, not to site traffic alone, then the stunt is judged on whether it actually paid for itself.

signal.check: A stunt's success is being reported as traffic or impressions with no comparison to incremental orders or contribution margin.

expected_effect.size: a founder claim states a $50,000 stunt can earn the reach of a $50 million TV buy; unaudited and not a rate to plan against

risk.note: A measurement and budgeting framework, not a live change.

prerequisites: An earned-media valuation method approved by the owner
steps: Write the earned-media valuation method before launch and get the owner's approval.
Budget the stunt's full cost against the marketing line.
Track incremental orders vs a matched prior window, not raw traffic.
Pass only if earned media value plus incremental contribution is worth more than the spend.

test.method: Compare incremental orders and contribution margin vs a matched window, alongside earned media value.

title: Cap wild-swing stunts to once or twice a year
hypothesis: If big stunts are capped to once or twice a year, with a second one only allowed after the first passes its earned-media mark, then the format stays special instead of wearing out the audience with repetition.

signal.check: More than one or two big stunts are planned for the same year, or a second stunt is planned without checking whether the first one passed.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources give conflicting frequency guidance (once or twice a year vs up to 4 a season); this playbook follows the once-or-twice text unless the owner decides otherwise

risk.note: A planning cap, not a live change.

prerequisites: A registry of past stunts and their pass/fail status
steps: Plan for one big stunt in the quarterly and annual plan by default.
Allow a second only if the first passed its earned-media mark.
Never draft a third without the owner's explicit decision.
Record the choice and reasoning in the registry.

test.method: Track stunt count per year against the cap.

title: Run a legal, ethics and brand-risk review before any stunt
hypothesis: If a stunt goes through a legal, ethics and brand-risk review before launch, including who could be offended and what happens if the joke lands flat, then the brand catches a foreseeable problem before it becomes a public one.

signal.check: A stunt is close to launch with no documented review of legal, contest, paid-participation or platform rules, and no written failure case.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives this review, it is a card addition to fill a real gap

risk.note: Skipping this review risks a real legal or reputational problem after a stunt cannot be withdrawn.

prerequisites: A confirmed stunt format and script
steps: Review contest, paid-participation and platform rules relevant to the stunt.
Write the failure case: who could be offended, and what happens if the joke lands flat.
Confirm site and stock capacity for a viral spike.
Get sign-off from the owner before launch, with the review attached to the approval request.

test.method: Not a performance test; a pre-launch compliance and risk gate.

title: Replace a planned discount sale with a gift-with-purchase, bundle or price hold
hypothesis: If a planned sale is replaced with a gift-with-purchase, a bundle, or a price hold framed as a promotion, then the brand avoids training loyal customers to wait for the next discount and raising their price sensitivity.
does_not_apply_when: A commodity category where units may need promotional pricing to move at all

signal.check: The default plan for an upcoming sale event is a blanket percentage-off discount, with no gift, bundle or price-hold alternative considered.

expected_effect.size: sources argue heavy discounting disillusions loyal customers and raises price sensitivity; no direct swap-vs-sale figure given

risk.note: A commodity category may see units collapse without the discount; watch closely and revert if needed.

prerequisites: Margin and unit data from the same sale event last year for comparison
steps: Pull margin and units from the same sale event last year as a baseline.
Design a gift-with-purchase, bundle, or price hold as the replacement offer.
Run it in place of the discount for this cycle.
Compare margin and units against the baseline; revert if units collapse in a commodity category.

test.method: Compare margin and units vs the same sale event last year.
test.read_point: At the close of the sale window

title: Pair any values or sustainability message with a real program that backs it
hypothesis: If a sustainability or quality message is only published once a real program (repair, resale, or an equivalent) exists behind it, then customers see it as genuine instead of marketing that invites greenwashing accusations.
does_not_apply_when: No repair, resale or equivalent program exists yet

signal.check: A values or sustainability message is planned with no repair, resale or similar program to point to.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source's case (an anti-consumption ad backed by repair and resale) is an example, not a rate

risk.note: A values message without a real program behind it can draw public backlash.

prerequisites: A documented repair, resale or equivalent program
steps: Confirm a real program (repair, resale, take-back) exists and is documented before writing the message.
Cite the program directly in the message so it is not just an assertion.
Run the legal, ethics and brand-risk review before publishing.
Track sentiment and complaints after publishing.

test.method: Monitor sentiment and complaint volume after the message goes live.

title: Run a guerrilla event where the exact target customers already gather
hypothesis: If a guerrilla activation goes where the exact target customers already gather, solves a real attendee pain, and secures venue permits first, then it creates a tangible, shareable moment instead of an ambush that draws the wrong kind of attention.

signal.check: A guerrilla or event idea exists with no venue permit plan and no clear match to where the actual target customer gathers.

expected_effect.size: case examples report selling out inventory within a week at a festival, and a branded truck at another event with no numbers given; attribution is weak

risk.note: Running without venue permits can create legal exposure or get the activation shut down.

prerequisites: Venue permits obtained
Travel and stock budget capped
steps: Pick a venue or event where the exact target customer already gathers.
Design something tangible and surprising, or solve an attendee pain point (heat, lines, discomfort).
Obtain venue permissions before the event.
Sell on the spot where possible and carry the moment to digital content afterward.

test.method: Track on-site sales, new customers with an event code, and social posts.
test.read_point: At the event and 2 weeks after

title: Run a mystery-first phased reveal only with distribution and stock ready for the payoff
hypothesis: If a mystery-first campaign (anonymous placement, then a message, then the reveal) only launches once distribution and stock are confirmed ready, then curiosity converts into sales instead of into a stockout or a flat payoff that annoys people.

signal.check: A mystery or teaser campaign is planned with no confirmed inventory or fulfillment capacity for the reveal date.

expected_effect.size: one case reports 395 clicks to a retail partner and 17,000 likes on the reveal; not a rate for a small store

risk.note: A weak payoff or a stockout at reveal can annoy the audience and, on some platforms, draw a policy penalty.

prerequisites: Inventory and fulfillment capacity confirmed before the reveal date
Brand voice supports playful or daring content
steps: Plan the 3 phases: anonymous placement, then a message, then the full reveal.
Confirm inventory and fulfillment capacity before locking the reveal date.
Only run this for brands whose voice supports playful or daring content.
Track reveal-day traffic and sales at the point of distribution.

test.method: Track reveal-day traffic and sales, and watch for platform-policy flags or negative reaction.
test.read_point: At the reveal and 1 week after

title: Own a topic the category avoids, with authenticity, on the platform the audience already talks
hypothesis: If a brand authentically and sensitively owns a topic its category usually avoids, on the platform where that audience already talks, then it can win attention and lower acquisition cost versus other media, subject to platform policy limits on sensitive claims.
does_not_apply_when: The topic touches health claims that would run into platform policy restrictions

signal.check: The category avoids a topic customers clearly care about, and the brand has not tested owning it authentically.

expected_effect.size: one case reports CPA 40% lower than other media and qualified leads up 42%, with a revenue figure that is ambiguous in the source

risk.note: Health-adjacent or sensitive claims face platform policy limits; check before running.

prerequisites: Platform health-adjacent or sensitive-content policy checked
steps: Identify a topic the category avoids that the target audience clearly cares about.
Check platform policy for any sensitive-content or health-claim restrictions.
Create content that owns the topic authentically and sensitively.
Track CPA against other channels running in parallel.

test.method: Compare CPA and qualified-lead rate against other running channels.

title: Turn a flat functional benefit into a jingle, character or cultural line and test it
hypothesis: If a plain functional benefit gets turned into a jingle, character or cultural line and tested against the plain functional version, then the brand learns whether memorability actually beats a flat feature claim for this audience.

signal.check: All current messaging states the functional benefit plainly with no memorable creative device tested against it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the cited case (a grocery app jingle) gives no numbers

risk.note: A creative test; low risk since both versions run as an A/B.

prerequisites: A creative team or resource to produce the alternate version
steps: Pick one functional benefit currently stated plainly.
Create a jingle, character or cultural-line version of the same claim.
Run both versions as an A/B test in the same channel.
Compare engagement and conversion between the two.

test.method: A/B test the plain vs the creative version.
test.read_point: After a statistically meaningful sample in each version

title: Launch an absurdist limited product only if the brand voice can carry it
hypothesis: If an absurdist or joke product only launches for brands whose voice already supports playfulness, then it shows personality that fits instead of confusing an audience expecting a serious brand.
does_not_apply_when: A serious or considered-purchase brand voice

signal.check: An absurdist or joke product idea is being considered for a brand with a serious, considered-purchase voice.

expected_effect.size: one case (an April Fool's-style limited product) reportedly sold out; quantity not given

risk.note: A limited, time-boxed product; low ongoing risk.

prerequisites: Owner confirmation that the brand voice supports playfulness
steps: Confirm with the owner that the brand voice actually supports an absurdist or joke product.
Design the product and its limited run with a clear time box.
Launch with clear framing that it is a limited, playful item.
Track sell-through and social reaction.

test.method: Track sell-through rate and social mentions during the limited run.
test.read_point: During and 1 week after the limited run

title: Fund an event-linked promotion's maximum payout in cash before launch
hypothesis: If a refund or freebie promotion tied to a binary event (a sports result, a market move) has its maximum possible payout fully funded in cash before launch, with any hedge treated as optional upside, then the store can honor every promise it makes without depending on an unverified bet.

signal.check: A promotion tied to an event outcome is being planned with the payout covered by an unverified hedge instead of cash on hand.

expected_effect.size: one case's hedge returned $13,514 on a $5,000 stake (2.70x); this is context for the hedge, not the promotion's own lift

risk.note: A public promise once made must be honored; fund it fully before announcing.

prerequisites: Legal review of promotion terms and any risk transfer
Order volume forecast for the event window
steps: Pick an event customers care about with a clear, binary outcome.
Define eligibility, qualifying orders, the outcome and the refund formula.
Calculate maximum refund exposure and cap the scope so it fits cash on hand.
Get legal review of the terms and any risk transfer before launch.
Track qualifying orders daily against the cap during the event window.

test.method: Track incremental orders vs the same window last year or a matched period, and realized payout vs the cap.

title: Run a bounded no-ads week and use the time for personal outreach
hypothesis: If paid acquisition pauses for one bounded week with a pre-set maximum acceptable revenue loss, while the team personally contacts lapsed customers, potential partners and micro-influencers, then organic dependence gets measured and the freed time turns into direct outreach instead of going to waste.
does_not_apply_when: A peak sales week, where the revenue loss risk is too high to test this way

signal.check: The store has never measured what happens to revenue when paid acquisition stops, and has 12 months of weekly organic vs paid data available.

expected_effect.size: one case ran with no paid ads for 5 years; its revenue figure is unclear in the source and should not be quoted

risk.note: Paid can restart any time if the loss cap is hit mid-week; watch for post-restart delivery disruption.

prerequisites: 12 months of weekly organic vs paid revenue
A maximum acceptable revenue loss set in advance
A week outside peak season
steps: Set the maximum acceptable revenue loss before the week starts.
Pick a week outside peak season and record the paid baseline.
Pause paid acquisition for 7 days; during the week, personally contact lapsed customers, potential partners and micro-influencers.
Measure organic traffic, orders and revenue during and for 4 weeks after, against the prior 4 weeks and the same week last year.
Record any delivery disruption or learning-phase reset after restarting paid.

test.method: Compare organic revenue share, reactivations, and paid recovery time after restart.
test.read_point: 7 days plus 4 weeks of read after

title: Replace an instant discount pop-up with a segmenting question first
hypothesis: If the pop-up asks a segmenting question before offering an incentive, then the store captures a useful zero-party answer while still converting, instead of handing out a blind discount to everyone.

signal.check: The current pop-up jumps straight to a flat percent-off offer with no segmenting question first.

expected_effect.size: presented as a framework in the source, not a tested win; no lift figure given

risk.note: A pop-up redesign; easy to revert.

prerequisites: A pop-up or quiz tool that supports a question step
steps: Replace the instant discount step with a short segmenting question (for example, a category or use-case choice).
Show a relevant incentive after the answer, tailored to the segment.
Store the answer as zero-party data for later use in gifts and support cues.
A/B test against the current instant-discount pop-up.

test.method: A/B test question-first vs instant-discount pop-up.

title: Decide the giveaway consolation offer before the giveaway ends
hypothesis: If the follow-up message to giveaway non-winners is decided before the giveaway ends, uses accurate and permitted wording, and tracks a real code, then non-winners get a genuine reason to buy without the brand overpromising or leaking margin through an uncontrolled code.

signal.check: A giveaway is planned or running with no decided follow-up plan for non-winners.

expected_effect.size: one case sent a discount DM to non-winners; no result given

risk.note: Watch for a leaked code eroding margin beyond the intended audience.

prerequisites: Platform DM and giveaway policy checked
steps: Decide the consolation offer and wording before the giveaway ends.
Confirm messaging is permitted on the platform (DM limits, automation rules).
Use accurate eligibility and expiry wording; never call a code 'secret' or 'exclusive' unless it is.
Track conversion from the message and watch for code leakage.

test.method: Track conversion from the consolation message and any signs of code leakage.

title: Fix the category's known failure point with an unglamorous premium component
hypothesis: If the product fixes a known, boring failure point of the category with a premium component (better wheels, a reinforced part) instead of chasing flashy features, then it wins on the thing customers actually complain about.

signal.check: Customer reviews or returns repeatedly cite the same known category failure point (a part that breaks, a feature that looks good but fails in use), and the product has not addressed it.

expected_effect.size: one case (a travel-bag brand) cites specific component upgrades and dropped low-value features; no unit economics given

risk.note: A product change; belongs to product development, with real tooling and inventory cost.

prerequisites: Return and review data identifying the category's known failure point
steps: Pull return reasons and review complaints to find the category's known failure point.
Identify a premium, unglamorous component that fixes it.
Cut a feature that markets well but fails in real use, if one exists.
Track defect rate and review sentiment after the change ships.

test.method: Compare defect rate and review sentiment before and after the component change.
test.read_point: 90 days after the updated product ships

title: Find a micro-channel or moment-based niche to be the only premium option in
hypothesis: If the brand finds a small, moment-based distribution channel where it can be the only premium option at the exact time of need, then it captures demand with little competition, judged on contribution margin after fees.

signal.check: A moment-based need exists near the product category (a last-minute travel need, an event tie-in) with no premium option currently distributing there.

expected_effect.size: case examples (a quick-commerce placement, a baggage-allowance tie-in) give no unit economics

risk.note: Verify partnership terms still run before committing; small distribution deals can end quietly.

prerequisites: A channel or partnership fee structure confirmed
steps: Identify a moment-based need adjacent to the product category with no premium option currently serving it.
Confirm the channel or partnership's fee structure and requirements.
Launch a small, reversible test in that channel.
Judge on contribution margin after fees, not just gross sales.

test.method: Track contribution margin after channel fees for the test period.
test.read_point: 60 to 90 days after the channel test starts

title: Over-invest in removing the category's biggest trust barrier
hypothesis: If the brand identifies the single biggest trust barrier to buying its category online (a big-ticket item sight unseen, a rug bought without touching it) and over-invests in removing it (education, photography, transparent specs), then conversion improves for a category that customers are naturally wary of.

signal.check: The category has a well-known trust barrier to buying online, and the store's current PDP or content does little to specifically address it.

expected_effect.size: case examples describe named businesses reaching large revenue by addressing their category's trust barrier; the exact measures behind the figures are unclear

risk.note: A content and education investment; low direct risk.

prerequisites: A clearly named trust barrier for the category
steps: Name the single biggest trust barrier customers have buying this category online.
Build education content, detailed photography, video, or transparent specs directly addressing it.
Place this content at the point of hesitation (PDP, cart, or a dedicated guide).
Track PDP-to-cart conversion before and after.

test.method: Compare PDP-to-cart conversion before and after the trust-barrier content launches.

title: Test a new country through an existing platform before building local infrastructure
hypothesis: If a new country is tested through an existing platform's cross-border features before any local infrastructure is built, and the entry is kept reversible, then the store learns real demand without committing capital to a market that may not work.

signal.check: A new-country expansion plan starts with local infrastructure (warehousing, entity setup) before testing demand through an existing platform.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the cited case names a platform-first path with no unit economics given

risk.note: Keep the entry reversible; verify eligibility, fulfilment, payments and fees before committing further.

prerequisites: Platform cross-border eligibility, fulfilment, payments and fees verified for the target country
steps: Verify the platform's cross-border eligibility, fulfilment, payment and fee terms for the target country.
Launch a small product set through the platform rather than building local infrastructure first.
Keep the entry reversible: no long-term local commitments yet.
Judge on contribution margin after fees before any further investment.

test.method: Track order volume and contribution margin after fees for the platform-first test.

title: Validate demand with a crowdfunding or pre-order campaign before committing to inventory
hypothesis: If a new product's demand is validated through crowdfunding or pre-orders, with an existing audience and stated delivery timelines, before committing to full inventory, then cash is not tied up in stock that might not sell.
does_not_apply_when: No existing audience to launch the campaign to

signal.check: A new product is about to be fully manufactured and stocked with no pre-order or crowdfunding step to validate demand first.

expected_effect.size: one case reports very large campaign GMV within hours; not a transferable benchmark for a small store

risk.note: Delivery timelines must be honestly stated; a delay risk is real and should be disclosed.

prerequisites: An existing audience to launch the campaign to
Realistic delivery timelines
steps: Set a funding or pre-order target and a stated, realistic delivery timeline.
Launch the campaign to the existing audience, not cold traffic.
Track funded units against the target at the campaign midpoint.
Stop or rework the plan if funding is well below target at the midpoint, before committing to full inventory.

test.method: Track funded units vs the target, checked at the campaign midpoint and close.
test.read_point: At the campaign midpoint and close

title: Personally walk the return, cancellation and broken-item paths as a customer would
hypothesis: If someone on the team personally walks the return, cancellation and broken-item support paths as a real customer would, then channel switches, repeated explanations and long waits get caught by direct experience instead of only by after-the-fact metrics.

signal.check: The base-effort audit relies only on aggregate metrics (CES, resolution time) with no one having personally walked the actual support paths.
